setup.text: Vote → holds a share; shareholder AND no defaulted loan → dividend; Okonkwo voted.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Okonkwo voted → holds a share. Shareholders get the dividend unless they have a defaulted loan. So the only gap is: Okonkwo has no defaulted loan. We need something that gets from 'voted' to 'no default.' Voted → no default. Contrapositive: default → can't vote. That's C.

choices.note: Wrong. Dividend → can vote. That runs backward from what we need.
Wrong. Already follows from the premises (he voted, so he holds a share). It leaves the default question open.
CORRECT. Default → can't vote. Contrapositive: voted → no default. Okonkwo voted, so no defaulted loan, and as a shareholder, he gets the dividend.
Wrong. Okonkwo might hold only one share. This tells you nothing about a single-share holder.
Wrong. The strongest trap. Can't vote → default. That's the reversal. It says nothing about members who did vote, like Okonkwo.

questions.stimulus: None of the translations of Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year is eligible for the Corwen Prize. After all, the prize's rules exclude any translation made from a relay text, that is, from an existing translation in a third language. And every translation Ilmar published this year was made from a relay text unless its translator holds a state certificate in the source language. Admittedly, Ilmar employs several certified translators, so some of its translations this year may well be eligible; but that does not alter the case of its Vessk poetry.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: No translator who holds a state certificate in Vessk translated any of the Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year.
Most of the Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year was translated by people who hold no state certificate in Vessk.
Every translation that Ilmar Press published this year by a certified translator was made directly from its source language.
Any translation made directly from its source language rather than from a relay text is eligible for the Corwen Prize.
Every translator Ilmar Press employed this year who lacks a state certificate in the source language worked from a relay text.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'no X is Y' statement that, through an 'unless' premise, completes a chain to a conclusion stated first. The premises say that any Ilmar translation this year whose translator lacks a certificate in the source language was made from a relay text, and relay translations are ineligible. So the conclusion follows if no Vessk-certified translator did any of Ilmar's Vessk poetry, as (A) says. (B) is the near-miss: it differs by one quantifier, and 'most' leaves room for some Vessk poetry by certified translators, which could be eligible. (C) is tempting because it reads 'unless' as a biconditional and echoes the concession, but even if certified translators always work directly from the source, nothing yet shows that none of the Vessk poetry was done by one. (D) reverses the eligibility rule, and (E) merely restates the premise about uncertified translators.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of Ilmar Press's Vessk poetry translations this year is eligible for the Corwen Prize.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Relay-text translation → ineligible; Ilmar translation this year AND translator lacks a source-language certificate → relay text; (concession: some Ilmar translators are certified).

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Vessk poetry by an uncertified translator → relay text → ineligible. The gap: what about Vessk poetry by a Vessk-certified translator? We need there to be none. So: Vessk poetry → translator not Vessk-certified. Then every piece runs → relay → ineligible.

choices.note: CORRECT. No Vessk-certified translator did any of Ilmar's Vessk poetry. So every piece had an uncertified translator → relay text → ineligible. Conclusion follows.
Wrong. The near-miss. 'Most' leaves room for some Vessk poetry by certified translators, which might be eligible. The conclusion says none.
Wrong. Tempting because it echoes the concession. But it still doesn't tell you whether any Vessk poetry was done by a certified translator. If some was, it might be eligible.
Wrong. Direct → eligible reverses the rule (relay → ineligible), and it can only help show eligibility, the opposite of the conclusion.
Wrong. Just restates the premise about uncertified translators. The gap is the certified ones.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, the town of Pell replaced the asphalt in all of its public parking lots with permeable paving, which allows rainwater to pass through it into the soil below. Since then, the peak flow of Marrow Creek, which drains the town, has been roughly 20 percent lower after heavy storms than it was before the change. Hydrologists in Pell conclude that the new paving is responsible for the reduction in the creek's storm peaks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Permeable paving is considerably more expensive to install than conventional asphalt.
The firm that installed Pell's permeable paving has completed similar projects in many other towns.
In several other towns that replaced asphalt lots with permeable paving, storm peaks in the local creeks dropped by similar amounts afterward.
Pell's residents voted by a wide margin in favor of replacing the asphalt lots.
Storms in the Marrow Creek watershed over the past three years have been, on average, less intense than those of the preceding decade.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the choice that directly supports the causal conclusion by showing the same cause produces the same effect elsewhere. C does exactly that: repeated cases in which permeable paving was followed by similar drops in storm peaks make it more likely that the paving, not chance, explains Pell's drop. The tempting trap is B, which also mentions other towns, but it tells us only that the installer was busy, not what happened to any creek. E is the wrong-direction trap: gentler storms are an alternative explanation for lower peaks, so it weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The permeable paving is responsible for the drop in Marrow Creek's storm peaks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pell replaced all its asphalt lots with permeable paving three years ago; since then, the creek's peak flow after heavy storms has been about 20 percent lower.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after causal claim. One way to strengthen: show the same cause gets the same effect in other places. If paving keeps being followed by lower creek peaks town after town, coincidence gets hard to believe. Like: every time you cut caffeine, your headaches go away. Once is luck; five times is a pattern. Prephrase: other towns that switched saw similar drops.

choices.note: Wrong. Cost has nothing to do with whether the paving lowered creek peaks. The LSAT is ultra specific: this is about cause, not cost.
Wrong. The trap. It mentions other towns, but only tells you the installer was busy. Nothing about what happened to those towns' creeks.
CORRECT. Same cause, same effect, in several places. That makes it more likely the paving, not chance, explains Pell's drop.
Wrong. How residents voted doesn't affect whether the paving worked.
Wrong. Opposite direction. Gentler storms are another explanation for lower peaks, so this weakens.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Fernhollow Press redesigned its long-running early-reader series, switching to larger type and adding an illustration to every page. In the twelve months after the redesigned books appeared, sales of the series rose by 30 percent over the previous twelve months. Fernhollow's editors conclude that the redesign made the series more appealing to young readers and the parents who buy books for them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Sales of other publishers' early-reader series, none of which changed their designs, stayed roughly flat over the same twelve months.
Fernhollow also substantially increased its advertising for the series last year.
Printing a book with an illustration on every page costs Fernhollow more than its previous format did.
Reading specialists disagree about whether frequent illustrations help or hinder beginning readers in learning to decode words.
Fernhollow plans to apply the same redesign to its chapter-book series next year.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a before-and-after causal claim by ruling out an alternative cause. A shows the whole early-reader market did not grow, so the 30 percent rise cannot be explained by a general boom and is more plausibly due to Fernhollow's change. The most tempting trap is D, because it is about the redesign's features, but the conclusion is about appeal to buyers, not about whether the illustrations teach reading well; a disagreement among specialists bears on neither. B is a weakener, offering advertising as a rival cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The redesign made Fernhollow's early-reader series more appealing to young readers and the parents who buy for them.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fernhollow switched to larger type and an illustration per page; sales rose 30 percent over the next twelve months.

breakdown.analysis: Sales went up after the redesign. But maybe the whole market went up, say because of a new reading initiative in schools. To strengthen, rule that out. Best tool: a comparison group. If competitors who didn't redesign stayed flat, the market wasn't booming, and the redesign looks responsible. Prephrase: other early-reader series didn't grow.

choices.note: CORRECT. Other publishers' unchanged series stayed flat. So there was no general boom to explain the 30 percent rise, which points to Fernhollow's redesign.
Wrong. Weakens. More advertising is a rival explanation for higher sales.
Wrong. Printing cost doesn't affect whether the redesign made the books more appealing.

Wrong. The tempting trap, since it's about the illustrations. But the conclusion is about appeal to buyers, not whether illustrations help kids learn to decode. A debate among specialists doesn't touch sales appeal.
Wrong. Future plans don't show the past redesign caused anything.

questions.stimulus: Volunteers at the Carrow Point banding station caught and banded 2,400 migrating warblers this autumn, and only 9 percent of them were first-year birds hatched that summer. A decade ago, first-year birds made up about 25 percent of the warblers banded at the station each autumn. The station's director concludes that the breeding success of the warbler populations that migrate past Carrow Point has declined sharply over the past decade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Adult warblers are better than first-year warblers at avoiding the mist nets used at banding stations.
Many of the warblers banded at Carrow Point this autumn were later recaptured at stations farther south.
The number of volunteers working at the station has roughly doubled over the past decade.
First-year warblers are generally lighter than adults when they pass Carrow Point.
Throughout the past decade, the station has operated its nets at the same locations and during the same weeks each autumn.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen by confirming that the samples being compared are comparable, so the change in the numbers reflects a change in the birds rather than in the sampling. E rules out the possibility that moved nets or shifted dates caught a different mix of ages this year than a decade ago. The tempting trap is A, which is about sampling bias and so feels on point; but a bias that is the same every year affects both figures alike and cannot explain why the share of young birds fell. C mentions a change at the station, but more volunteers banding the same nets would not change the age mix.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Breeding success of warblers migrating past Carrow Point has declined sharply over the past decade.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: This autumn, 9 percent of 2,400 banded warblers were first-year birds; a decade ago, about 25 percent were.

breakdown.analysis: The director compares two samples. That only works if the samples were caught the same way. If the nets moved or the dates shifted, you might be catching a different mix of birds, say, young birds migrating earlier and being missed. Like comparing class average scores when one year's test was easier. Prephrase: the station sampled the same way both times.

choices.note: Wrong. The trap. It's a sampling bias, but the same bias every year affects both figures equally. It can't explain why the share of young birds fell.
Wrong. Where the birds got recaptured later says nothing about how many young birds there are.
Wrong. More volunteers working the same nets would band more birds, but wouldn't change the age mix. Doesn't help the argument.
Wrong. Weight differences don't bear on whether the share of young birds reflects breeding success.
CORRECT. Same nets, same places, same weeks every year. That rules out a sampling change, so the drop in young birds likely reflects a real change in the population.

questions.stimulus: At Halvard Clinic, patients whose knee replacements were done with the Corin technique, which preserves a thigh-muscle tendon that the standard technique cuts, walked unassisted an average of nine days sooner than patients given the standard technique. Admittedly, surgeons chose which technique to use, and they tended to use the Corin technique on younger patients. But even among patients under sixty, those given the Corin technique walked unassisted sooner. So the faster recovery is attributable to the preservation of the tendon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Younger patients generally regain mobility after knee replacement faster than older patients do.
When the tendon is cut, the thigh muscle it anchors cannot generate enough force to stabilize the knee during walking until the tendon has reattached, which takes about a week.
The Corin technique also requires a somewhat smaller incision than the standard technique does.
Most surgeons who have tried the Corin technique now prefer it to the standard technique.
Patients under sixty make up only a small fraction of the clinic's knee-replacement patients.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen by supplying the mechanism that links the specific feature named in the conclusion (the tendon) to the effect. The premises at most show the Corin technique helps; B explains how cutting the tendon would delay walking by about the observed amount, which makes the tendon, rather than some other feature of the technique, the likely cause. The strongest trap is A: it supports the concession about age, which the argument already answered with the under-sixty comparison, so it adds nothing to the conclusion and if anything highlights a confound. D supports a different conclusion (that the technique is better overall), and C offers a rival feature, so it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The faster recovery is attributable to preserving the tendon.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corin-technique patients walked unassisted nine days sooner on average; surgeons used Corin more on younger patients, but even among under-60 patients, Corin patients walked sooner.

breakdown.analysis: The premises show the Corin technique helps. But the conclusion is narrower: the tendon is the reason. The technique might differ in other ways. To strengthen, connect the tendon specifically to the faster walking. A mechanism does that: cut tendon → weak muscle → can't walk until it reattaches in about a week. That's about the gap observed.

choices.note: Wrong. The strongest trap. It supports the age concern, which the argument already answered with the under-60 comparison. It adds nothing, and if anything highlights the confound.

CORRECT. Mechanism. Cutting the tendon leaves the muscle unable to stabilize the knee until it reattaches, about a week. That explains how the tendon itself delays walking by roughly the observed amount.
Wrong. Weakens. A smaller incision is another difference between the techniques that could explain faster recovery.
Wrong. Surgeon preference supports the idea that the technique is better, not that the tendon is the reason.
Wrong. If under-60 patients are only a small fraction, the under-60 comparison is less convincing. That doesn't help.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Brenford restaurants in the western districts, now inspected by unannounced teams, averaged 4.1 recorded violations per inspection, while those in the eastern districts, still inspected on a schedule announced a week ahead, averaged 2.3. Some council members take this as evidence that western restaurants are less sanitary. Granted, the western districts contain more of the city's older buildings. But scheduled inspections are known to understate violations, since restaurants can prepare for them. So the council members' inference is unwarranted, and if unannounced inspections were extended to the east, recorded violations there would likely approach the western level.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Restaurants that learn of an inspection a week in advance typically use that time to correct problems an inspector would otherwise cite.
Unannounced inspections are more effective than scheduled ones at reducing the incidence of foodborne illness.
Older restaurant buildings are more difficult to keep free of pests than newer ones are.
Four years ago, before unannounced inspections began, western and eastern restaurants averaged nearly identical numbers of recorded violations per scheduled inspection.
Several eastern-district restaurants have voluntarily requested unannounced inspections in order to reassure customers.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a comparison by establishing a baseline, an answer that looks like irrelevant history on first read. D shows that when both halves of the city were measured the same way, they looked the same; so the current gap appeared with the change in method, which supports both that the gap is not about sanitation (despite the older buildings) and that eastern numbers would rise under the new method. The main trap is A: it feels like strong support, but it only restates a premise the argument already gives (scheduled inspections understate violations because restaurants prepare), and it says nothing about how large the understatement is relative to the gap. B supports a different conclusion, a policy recommendation the author never makes, and C strengthens the conceded alternative, so it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council members' inference that western restaurants are less sanitary is unwarranted, and unannounced inspections in the east would likely bring violations up near the western level.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: West (unannounced) averaged 4.1 violations; east (announced a week ahead) averaged 2.3; scheduled inspections understate violations since restaurants prepare; (concession: the west has more older buildings).

breakdown.analysis: The author blames the gap on the inspection method, not on dirtier restaurants. Best support: show the gap appeared when the method changed. If both halves of the city scored the same back when both had scheduled inspections, the older buildings weren't making a difference, and the method is the likely reason for today's gap. It's like two classes scoring the same on a take-home test, then one gets a pop quiz and scores lower. The quiz, not the class, made the difference.

choices.note: Wrong. Feels like strong support, but it just restates a premise: scheduled inspections understate violations because restaurants prepare. It says nothing about how big that effect is compared to the gap.
Wrong. Supports a different conclusion, a policy recommendation the author never makes. Foodborne illness isn't the issue.
Wrong. Weakens. It supports the conceded alternative: older western buildings may really be less sanitary.

CORRECT. Before the method changed, east and west scored nearly the same. So the gap showed up with the new method, not because of the buildings, and eastern numbers would likely rise under the same method.
Wrong. Some eastern restaurants asking for unannounced inspections says nothing about what those inspections would find.

questions.stimulus: Since the Tallow Ridge wind farm began operating two years ago, crews inspecting the ground beneath its forty turbines have found dozens of dead bats each late summer, far more than they find in any other season. The ridge lies on a known migration route for several bat species. Local conservationists conclude that the turbines' spinning blades are killing bats that fly over the ridge during their seasonal migration.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Many bat species in the region migrate during late summer and early autumn.
Examinations show that most of the dead bats found beneath the turbines died of a fungal disease that has recently spread through the region's bat colonies.
Wind turbines generate electricity without producing greenhouse gas emissions.
The turbines at Tallow Ridge are taller than those at most other wind farms in the region.
Dead bats have also been found beneath the turbines of several other wind farms.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a causal conclusion by giving a different cause for the observed effect. If most of the bats died of disease, the presence of carcasses under the turbines no longer shows the blades killed them. The tempting trap is E, because it is about dead bats at wind farms and so feels relevant; but it is consistent with turbines killing bats and, if anything, strengthens the conclusion. A merely supports the premise that bats pass by during migration.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The turbines' spinning blades are killing bats that fly over the ridge during migration.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the wind farm opened, crews find dozens of dead bats under the turbines each late summer, far more than in other seasons; the ridge is on a bat migration route.

breakdown.analysis: Dead bats under turbines looks damning. But location isn't cause of death. If the bats died of something else, the turbines are off the hook. It's like finding a body near a car and concluding it was a hit-and-run, before the autopsy shows a heart attack. Prephrase: the bats died of something else.

choices.note: Wrong. Just supports the premise that bats pass by during migration. Doesn't weaken.
CORRECT. Different cause of death. If most of the bats died of a fungal disease, finding them under the turbines no longer shows the blades killed them.
Wrong. Emissions are irrelevant to whether turbines kill bats.
Wrong. Taller turbines, if anything, might make collisions more likely. Doesn't weaken.
Wrong. The tempting trap. It's about dead bats at wind farms, but it fits with turbines killing bats and, if anything, strengthens.

questions.stimulus: When the Ashgrove Public Library eliminated overdue fines last year, the number of books returned late fell by 15 percent compared with the year before, even though the library lent out about the same number of books in both years. The library's director argues that fines had been discouraging timely returns, because borrowers who owed fines avoided the library, and that eliminating fines is what produced the decline in late returns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Eliminating fines cost the library a significant portion of its annual revenue.
Many borrowers surveyed last year said they had avoided the library in the past while they owed fines.
The 15 percent figure was compiled by library staff rather than by outside auditors.
At the same time it eliminated fines, the library began sending borrowers automated reminders a few days before their books were due.
Some borrowers who returned books late last year had also returned books late in earlier years.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a before-and-after argument by identifying a simultaneous change that could explain the result. Due-date reminders are an independent reason late returns would fall, so the decline no longer points to the fine policy. The tempting traps are A, which attacks the policy on a ground (revenue) the director never claims anything about, and C, which tries to cast doubt on the 15 percent figure, a premise we must accept as given. B actually strengthens the director's proposed mechanism.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating fines is what produced the 15 percent decline in late returns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year the library dropped overdue fines; late returns fell 15 percent with about the same number of books lent; fines had made borrowers who owed them avoid the library.

breakdown.analysis: Before-and-after reasoning. The weak point: anything else that changed at the same time. If the library also changed something that would directly cut late returns, the fine policy loses credit. Prephrase: something else happened at the same time that would reduce late returns.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting because it's a real downside, but the director never says anything about revenue. Cost isn't the question; cause is.
Wrong. Strengthens. It supports the director's mechanism that fines kept people away.
Wrong. Tempting, but it just casts vague doubt on the 15 percent figure, which you have to accept as given. Staff compiling it doesn't show it's wrong.
CORRECT. At the same moment fines ended, automated due-date reminders started. Reminders are an obvious reason late returns would fall, so the decline no longer points to the fine policy.
Wrong. Some repeat late returners existing doesn't explain or undercut the 15 percent drop.

questions.stimulus: An analysis of 3,000 listings on Drivemart, an online used-car marketplace, found that cars advertised with a complete set of service records sold for 12 percent more, on average, than cars of the same make, model, age, and mileage advertised without them. The analysts conclude that a seller who assembles complete service records before listing a car can expect to raise its sale price by about 12 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Owners who keep complete service records also tend to maintain their cars more carefully, so their cars are typically in better mechanical condition than comparable cars without records.
Cars sold through Drivemart typically fetch slightly higher prices than similar cars sold through dealerships.
Many buyers surveyed said that service records gave them confidence that a car had been well maintained.
Assembling a complete set of service records can take a seller many hours of work.
Some of the cars listed with complete service records had been in minor accidents.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a correlation-to-causation leap by showing the supposed cause is a marker for a hidden factor. If cars with records are simply better cars, the 12 percent premium reflects condition, and a seller who merely gathers paperwork for an ordinary car would not capture it. The most tempting trap is D, which attacks whether assembling records is worthwhile, a claim the analysts never make; their claim is only about the price increase. B is tempting as a representativeness worry, but a different price level across venues says nothing about the size of the percentage premium, and C strengthens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A seller who assembles complete service records before listing can expect about a 12 percent higher sale price.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Across 3,000 Drivemart listings, cars with complete service records sold for 12 percent more than cars of the same make, model, age, and mileage without them.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation, with a twist: the conclusion is about what happens if you go gather paperwork. But maybe records are a sign of something else, a well-cared-for car. People who keep records also change their oil. Buyers pay for the better car, not the folder. Like noticing people with gym memberships are fitter and concluding that buying a membership will make you fit. Prephrase: records go with better cars, so the premium comes from condition.

choices.note: CORRECT. Records are a marker for careful owners and better-maintained cars. The premium reflects condition. Gathering paperwork for an ordinary car won't get you 12 percent.
Wrong. A higher price level on Drivemart versus dealerships says nothing about the size of the percentage premium for records within Drivemart.
Wrong. Strengthens. Buyers say records give them confidence, which supports records themselves raising the price.
Wrong. The tempting trap. It attacks whether gathering records is worth the effort, but the analysts only claim it raises the price. Effort isn't part of the conclusion.
Wrong. Some record-holding cars having minor accidents doesn't explain away the premium. If anything, those cars still sold for more.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologists transplanted fragments of staghorn coral bred at the Ilsa Bay nursery onto a degraded section of the Varro Reef. Two years later, a marine heat wave struck; 70 percent of the transplanted fragments survived it, compared with 30 percent of the wild staghorn on an adjacent section. Admittedly, a few transplants were lost to storms before the heat wave, but these were excluded from the count. The result shows, the biologists say, that the nursery's breeding program has produced staghorn substantially more resistant to heat stress than wild staghorn.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Wild staghorn on other sections of the Varro Reef suffered losses in the heat wave similar to those on the adjacent section.
The transplanted fragments grew more slowly during their two years on the reef than wild staghorn on the adjacent section did.
Bleached but still-living staghorn can be hard to distinguish from dead coral, so divers' survival counts after heat waves are sometimes inaccurate.
The nursery's fragments were bred from parent colonies collected on the Varro Reef itself.

Before transplanting, the nursery grows all fragments in tanks whose temperature is gradually raised, a treatment known to boost any coral's heat tolerance for several years regardless of its parentage.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken by separating the factor the conclusion credits (breeding) from another feature of the same treatment (tank conditioning). The data show nursery corals survived better, but E supplies a non-genetic reason they would, so the result no longer shows the breeding program produced more heat-resistant corals. Two traps are strong: B attacks a claim the biologists never make (that the corals are better overall), and C tries to weaken the survival data, which are given as premises; besides, a counting difficulty applies to both groups and gives no reason to think the gap is exaggerated. A strengthens by showing the comparison group was typical.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The nursery's breeding program produced staghorn substantially more heat-resistant than wild staghorn.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years after transplanting, a heat wave hit; 70 percent of transplants survived versus 30 percent of adjacent wild staghorn; transplants lost to storms beforehand were excluded.

breakdown.analysis: The data show nursery corals survived better. The conclusion credits breeding, meaning genetics. But nursery corals differ in more than breeding: how they were raised. If the nursery's handling toughens any coral, the advantage isn't from breeding at all. Like crediting a racehorse's bloodline when it also had the best trainer. Prephrase: something else about the nursery made them tougher.

choices.note: Wrong. Strengthens. It shows the comparison group was typical, not unusually weak.
Wrong. A trap. Slower growth attacks a claim the biologists never make, that nursery coral is better overall. The conclusion is only about heat resistance.
Wrong. A trap. The survival data are premises you accept. And a counting problem would hit both groups alike, so it gives no reason to think the gap is exaggerated.
Wrong. Local parentage doesn't separate breeding from anything else. It doesn't undercut the breeding claim.

CORRECT. The nursery heat-conditions every fragment in tanks, and that boosts any coral's heat tolerance for years regardless of parentage. So the survival edge could come from conditioning, not breeding.

questions.stimulus: Since the Marlow Opera House began selling $20 rush tickets to patrons under thirty, 18 percent of its ticket buyers have been under thirty, compared with 7 percent at the Venn Opera, which offers no such discount. Venn's board had long believed that opera simply does not appeal to young adults. It now concludes that it was wrong: young adults will attend opera when it is affordable. Hence, the board reasons, a rush-ticket program at Venn would substantially increase the share of its ticket buyers who are under thirty.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Adults under thirty in Venn's city, when surveyed, most often cite ticket prices as their reason for not attending opera.
Some of Marlow's ticket buyers under thirty pay full price rather than buying rush tickets.
In the season before Marlow introduced rush tickets, 16 percent of its ticket buyers were already under thirty.
Marlow sells its rush tickets for less than it costs to fill each seat for a performance.
Venn's board originally adopted its view of young audiences on the basis of a survey conducted more than a decade ago.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken by undermining the comparison through its base rate. The argument treats the 18-versus-7 gap as the effect of rush tickets, but C shows Marlow's young share was already 16 percent before the program, so nearly all of the gap predates the discount and gives little reason to expect a program to transform Venn's numbers. The sneakiest trap is B, which hinges on a quantifier: if most young Marlow buyers paid full price, the discount would look irrelevant, but some paying full price is fully compatible with the program driving attendance. A strengthens, D attacks the program's finances (a claim never made), and E attacks the board's old belief, which the board has already abandoned.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A rush-ticket program at Venn would substantially increase its share of under-thirty ticket buyers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Marlow, with $20 rush tickets for under-thirties, has 18 percent under-thirty buyers; Venn, with no discount, has 7 percent; so young adults attend opera when it's affordable.

breakdown.analysis: The argument credits the 18-versus-7 gap to rush tickets. But what was Marlow's number before the program? If it was already high, the gap predates the discount, and something else about Marlow (its city, its programming) draws young people. It's like crediting a new coach for a team's winning record when they won just as much last year. Prephrase: Marlow already had lots of young buyers before rush tickets.

choices.note: Wrong. Strengthens. If young adults in Venn's city say price keeps them away, a discount should help.

Wrong. The sneakiest trap, hinging on 'some.' If most young Marlow buyers paid full price, the discount might look irrelevant. But some paying full price fits fine with the program driving attendance.

CORRECT. Marlow's young share was already 16 percent before rush tickets. So nearly all of the gap with Venn predates the program, which gives little reason to expect rush tickets to change Venn's numbers much.
Wrong. Attacks the program's finances. The board only claims it would increase young attendance, not that it pays for itself.
Wrong. Attacks the board's old belief, which the board has already abandoned. Doesn't touch the new conclusion.

questions.stimulus: The turbines at the Gorran Flats wind farm generate the most electricity in winter, when winds in the area are strongest, and the least in summer, when calm days are common. The farm sells all of its output to the regional grid and has no other significant source of income. Yet the wind farm's revenue from selling electricity to the regional grid is consistently highest in summer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Winds at Gorran Flats are stronger in every season than at most other wind farms in the region.
The farm's turbines need more frequent maintenance in winter, when ice forms on their blades.
Summer days are considerably longer than winter days at Gorran Flats's latitude.
The price the regional grid pays for each unit of electricity is several times higher in summer, when demand for air-conditioning peaks, than in winter.
Several new wind farms in the region began selling electricity to the grid last year.
questions.explanation: Core move: reconcile two facts by finding the missing variable that links them; here revenue depends on price as well as quantity. D shows that a smaller summer output sells at a much higher price, so summer revenue can exceed winter revenue. The tempting trap is B, which explains higher winter costs, but costs do not affect revenue, and the stimulus already says winter output is highest. C is irrelevant because turbines run on wind, not daylight.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The farm makes the most electricity in winter and sells all of it to the grid, but its revenue is highest in summer.

breakdown.analysis: Revenue isn't just how much you sell. It's how much you sell times the price. The stimulus only tells you about quantity, so the missing piece is almost certainly price. Prephrase: summer electricity sells for a lot more per unit. It's like a lemonade stand that sells fewer cups at a pricey festival than on a normal day, but still makes more money there.

choices.note: Irrelevant comparison. How Gorran Flats stacks up against other farms says nothing about why its own summer revenue beats its own winter revenue.
Trap. Maintenance is a cost, and costs don't touch revenue. Even if ice cut winter output a bit, the stimulus already says winter output is still the highest. So this explains nothing.
Irrelevant. Wind turbines run on wind, not sunlight. Longer days don't mean more wind or a better price.

CORRECT. If summer electricity sells for several times the winter price, a smaller summer output can bring in more money. Less volume times a much higher price beats more volume times a low price. Both facts now fit.
New competitors would affect the farm all year. Nothing here explains why summer in particular earns more. If anything, more supply might push prices down.

questions.stimulus: Bookstore sales of a picture book typically triple in the year after it wins the Brambling Medal, a prize awarded annually to one picture book and announced with considerable publicity. The county's libraries, like most, keep at least one copy of each winner on their shelves. Yet in Calder County's public libraries, medal-winning picture books are checked out less often in the year after winning than in the year before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Bookstores prominently display and promote medal winners in the months after the award is announced.
Many parents who learn that a picture book has won the medal buy a copy for their own household rather than borrowing it from a library.
The committee that selects the Brambling Medal winner is made up largely of children's librarians.
Picture books are checked out from Calder County's libraries more often than any other kind of children's book.
Some books that have won the Brambling Medal were already bestsellers before receiving it.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the one fact that connects the two trends, so that the rise in one actually produces the fall in the other. If families who once borrowed medal winners now buy them, the award drives sales up and library checkouts down simultaneously. The tempting trap is A: it explains the jump in bookstore sales but leaves the library decline unexplained. E concerns only a few books and explains neither trend.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Winning the Brambling Medal triples a book's bookstore sales, but in Calder County's libraries the winning books get checked out less after they win.

breakdown.analysis: You'd expect a famous prize to make a book more popular everywhere. So you want one fact that makes the sales jump and the library drop happen together. Prephrase: the people who used to borrow these books now buy them instead. It's like a hit movie coming out on streaming: more people watch it, but fewer rent the DVD from the library, because they don't need to.

choices.note: Half an explanation. Store promotion explains why bookstore sales rise, but not why library checkouts fall. The LSAT wants both sides of the paradox handled.
CORRECT. The medal sends parents to buy their own copies, and those parents stop borrowing. One mechanism drives sales up and checkouts down at the same time.
Who sits on the committee doesn't change anything after the award. This doesn't explain either trend.
This compares picture books to other children's books. It says nothing about why medal winners in particular get borrowed less after they win.
'Some' books is too weak, and being a bestseller before the award doesn't explain why checkouts would drop after it. Explains neither trend.

questions.stimulus: At Westmere Hospital last year, patients whose hip fractures were surgically repaired within 24 hours of admission had a higher rate of complications than patients whose surgery took place more than 48 hours after admission, even after the hospital accounted for differences in the patients' ages. Yet large studies consistently find that, for hip-fracture patients generally, delaying surgery increases the risk of complications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Complications associated with delayed surgery include blood clots and pneumonia, both of which can result from prolonged bed rest.
Westmere's surgeons perform more hip-fracture repairs each year than surgeons at most comparable hospitals do.
Most of the large studies of surgical timing were conducted at hospitals considerably larger than Westmere.
Hip fractures are much more common among elderly people than among younger people.
Westmere operates immediately mainly on patients with severe, displaced fractures, while patients with simple, stable fractures are scheduled later as operating rooms become free.
questions.explanation: Core move: resolve a conflict between a local result and a general finding by showing the local comparison groups differ. If Westmere's early-surgery group is made up of the hardest cases, it can have more complications even though, for any given patient, delay is harmful, so both facts stand. The most tempting trap is A, which explains why delay is generally harmful but does nothing to explain Westmere's reverse pattern. C is tempting because it hints Westmere is different, but hospital size alone gives no reason early surgery would go worse there.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: At Westmere, fast hip surgery (within 24 hours) led to more complications than slow surgery (after 48 hours), but big studies show delay generally raises complications.

breakdown.analysis: When a local result runs opposite to the general rule, ask whether the local groups are really comparable. Prephrase: Westmere's fast-surgery patients were sicker to begin with. Then early surgery can be better for each patient and the early group can still have more complications. It's like noticing that people who go to the ER by ambulance die more often than people who drive themselves. Ambulances aren't deadly; the sickest people take them.

choices.note: Trap. This explains why delay is usually harmful, which is the half of the paradox nobody doubted. It does nothing to explain why Westmere shows the reverse.
Lots of surgeries might make Westmere's surgeons skilled, but that would apply to fast and slow operations alike. It doesn't explain the reversed pattern.
Tempting because it hints Westmere is different. But size alone gives no reason early surgery would go worse at a smaller hospital. A difference isn't an explanation.
True of everyone, and the hospital already adjusted for age. This doesn't separate Westmere's early and late groups.

CORRECT. Westmere operates fast on the severe fractures and makes the easy cases wait. So the early group is loaded with hard cases and will have more complications anyway. Delay can still be harmful for any given patient. Both facts stand.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, live coral cover on the Selka Atoll's reefs has increased by about a third, reversing earlier losses. Over the same period, annual surveys have recorded a steady decline in the number of reef-fish species present at the atoll, and the decline has been as steep among species that no fishery targets as among commercially caught species. Since reef fish depend on corals for food and shelter, marine ecologists had expected the coral's recovery to bring a recovery in fish diversity.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The coral recovery has consisted almost entirely of a single fast-growing plating species, which has overgrown the branching corals whose complex shapes shelter many reef-fish species.
Commercial fishing around the atoll has intensified considerably over the past decade.
Since a ban on boat anchoring took effect ten years ago, damaged coral on the atoll has been steadily regrowing.
Many reef-fish species at the atoll feed mainly on algae rather than on coral itself.
The fish species that have disappeared from the atoll's surveys are still found on reefs elsewhere in the region.
questions.explanation: Core move: choose the answer that explains both facts at once and fits every detail of the stimulus, while traps explain only one side. A explains why coral cover rose (a fast-growing species spread) and why fish diversity fell (that spread destroyed the complex habitat many species need). B is the strongest trap, a natural explanation for fewer fish, but the stimulus already rules it out by noting that untargeted species declined just as steeply. C explains only the coral increase, and D at most weakens the ecologists' expectation without explaining why diversity actually declined.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Coral cover on the Selka Atoll reefs is up by a third, but the number of reef-fish species keeps falling, even though fish depend on coral.

breakdown.analysis: More coral should mean more fish species. So look for a reason the new coral isn't the kind that helps fish. Also notice the detail: untargeted species dropped just as fast as fished ones, so fishing is ruled out. Prephrase: the coral that came back is a different, less useful type. It's like a city that adds lots of parking lots: more paved area, but fewer places for people to live.

choices.note: CORRECT. The recovery is one fast-growing plating coral that has smothered the branching corals fish shelter in. That explains both facts at once: coral cover rose, and habitat for many fish species shrank.

The strongest trap. More fishing is a natural reason for fewer fish. But the stimulus already said species nobody fishes for declined just as steeply. Read every detail: the LSAT planted that line to kill this answer.
This explains only why coral recovered, which isn't the puzzle. It says nothing about why fish diversity fell.
At most this weakens the ecologists' expectation a little. Fish could still use coral for shelter, and it gives no reason diversity actually declined.
Where else the fish live doesn't explain why they disappeared from Selka. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Last season the Halvorsen Opera raised the price of every seat by about a quarter, expecting to sell fewer tickets but to earn more overall. Instead, the number of tickets it sold rose by 10 percent. Its audience surveys showed no change in the age or income of its patrons. Over the same season, the city's two other opera companies kept their prices unchanged, and both sold fewer tickets than the season before.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Many operagoers in the city treat a higher ticket price as a sign of a more lavish production, and Halvorsen's prices are now the highest in the city.
Halvorsen's season included several of the most popular works in the operatic repertory, whereas its competitors staged mostly unfamiliar operas.
Even before Halvorsen raised its prices, its tickets cost more than comparable seats at either of the other companies.
A celebrated tenor who had previously sung mainly with one of the other companies joined Halvorsen's company last season.
Halvorsen reopened last season in a renovated hall whose improved sightlines and acoustics drew widespread favorable press coverage.
questions.explanation: Core move: in an EXCEPT explain question, eliminate the four choices that resolve the discrepancy and find the one that only seems to. C sounds like an explanation because it is about relative price, but it only shows Halvorsen became even more expensive relative to rivals, which deepens the puzzle of why its sales rose while theirs fell. The most tempting trap is A, which looks odd enough to pick as the EXCEPT, but if patrons read high prices as a signal of quality, the price increase itself could draw buyers, so it does explain. B, D, and E each give patrons a reason to shift from the rivals to Halvorsen, explaining both Halvorsen's gain and the rivals' losses.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Halvorsen raised all its prices by a quarter and sold 10 percent more tickets, while its two rivals kept prices flat and sold fewer.

breakdown.analysis: This is an EXCEPT question: four answers explain the paradox, and the right answer doesn't. Anything that gives people a reason to switch from the rivals to Halvorsen helps. Watch for an answer that's about price but only makes Halvorsen look worse for buyers. That one deepens the puzzle instead of solving it.

choices.note: Helps, so it's wrong here. It looks strange enough to be the odd one out, but if operagoers read a high price as a sign of a lavish show, the price hike itself could pull in buyers. That explains the result.
Helps. Popular operas at Halvorsen and obscure ones elsewhere give people a reason to choose Halvorsen, explaining its gain and the rivals' losses.

CORRECT. This sounds like an explanation because it's about price, but it just says Halvorsen was already the expensive option and got even more expensive. That makes it even stranger that people chose it. It doesn't resolve anything.
Helps. A star tenor moving from a rival to Halvorsen could draw his fans along, raising Halvorsen's sales and lowering the rival's.
Helps. A newly renovated hall with great press is a reason to go to Halvorsen even at higher prices.

questions.stimulus: The water level in Brinley Reservoir fell sharply over the course of this summer, reaching its lowest point in more than twenty years. The reservoir is fed by streams draining the surrounding hills. The regional water authority attributes the drop to increased household water use by the residents of Brinley, a fast-growing town that draws all of its water from the reservoir.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether rainfall in the area that drains into Brinley Reservoir was much lower this summer than in previous summers
Whether most Brinley residents would support restrictions on lawn watering
When Brinley Reservoir was originally constructed
Whether other towns in the region also draw their water from reservoirs
Whether Brinley's population is expected to keep growing next year
questions.explanation: Core move: an evaluate question asks for the information whose answer would change how strong the argument is, and the obvious candidate is a rival cause. If rainfall was unusually low, drought could explain the drop and the argument weakens; if rainfall was normal, the household-use explanation gains ground. The tempting trap is E, since it concerns the town's growth, but future growth says nothing about what caused this summer's drop. B concerns a possible remedy, not the cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reservoir dropped because Brinley residents used more water.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The reservoir hit a 20-year low this summer; it's fed by streams from the hills; fast-growing Brinley draws all its water from it.

breakdown.analysis: The authority picked one cause, but a reservoir has two sides: water going out and water coming in. The stimulus even tells you it's fed by streams. Prephrase: was there less water coming in? That's the rival cause. It's like blaming your kids for an empty bank account without checking whether your paycheck stopped. A good evaluate answer gives you a question where one answer helps the argument and the other hurts it.

choices.note: CORRECT. If rain in the drainage area was way down, drought could explain the drop and the household-use story weakens. If rain was normal, household use looks like the likely cause. Either answer changes how strong the argument is.
This is about a possible fix, not the cause. Whether people would accept watering limits tells you nothing about why the water level fell.
When the reservoir was built doesn't bear on what happened this summer. Irrelevant.
Other towns' water sources don't matter unless they draw from this reservoir, and the question doesn't say they do.
Trap. It mentions growth, which sounds related. But next year's growth can't explain this summer's drop. Past cause, not future trend.

questions.stimulus: Since Corvel City began requiring restaurants to post their latest inspection grades in their front windows, reported cases of foodborne illness traced to restaurants have dropped by 20 percent compared with the year before the rule took effect. The number of restaurants in the city has stayed roughly constant. A city official argues that the posting requirement has motivated restaurants to improve their hygiene practices.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether restaurants with high posted grades charge higher prices than those with low grades
Whether some other cities post restaurant inspection grades online rather than in windows
Whether restaurants' average inspection scores have risen since the posting requirement took effect
Whether foodborne illness is generally more common in summer than in winter
Whether the posted grade signs are printed in more than one language
questions.explanation: Core move: test the official's mechanism directly. If inspection scores rose, there is independent evidence that hygiene improved, supporting the argument; if scores stayed flat, the drop in illness likely has some other cause, weakening it. The tempting trap is B, which is about grade posting, but how other cities publish grades says nothing about what happened in Corvel. D is tempting as a possible confound, but a seasonal pattern recurs every year and so cannot explain a year-over-year decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Posting inspection grades made restaurants improve their hygiene.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since posting began, restaurant foodborne illness reports dropped 20 percent; the number of restaurants stayed about the same.

breakdown.analysis: The official skips a step: illness dropped, so hygiene must have improved. The cleanest test is to check the middle link directly. Prephrase: did hygiene actually get better? Inspection scores measure exactly that. It's like crediting a new diet for weight loss: you'd want to know whether the person actually ate differently.

choices.note: Prices are irrelevant. Whether good-grade places charge more says nothing about whether hygiene improved.
Trap, because it's about posting grades. But how other cities post them tells you nothing about what happened in Corvel. The LSAT is ultra specific: stick to this city and this rule.

CORRECT. If scores went up, you have independent evidence hygiene improved, and the argument gets stronger. If scores stayed flat, the illness drop probably has another cause, and the argument weakens.
Tempting as a possible confound, but a seasonal pattern happens every year. Comparing one year to the year before already includes both seasons, so it can't explain the drop.
Sign languages might affect who reads them, but this doesn't test whether restaurants actually cleaned up. Too far from the argument.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Hartwell Motors, a used-car dealership, stopped negotiating prices and began posting a fixed, no-haggle price on every car. Its average profit per car sold rose by 8 percent compared with the year before. Previously, its salespeople had been free to cut prices during negotiations by whatever amount they judged necessary to close a sale. The dealership's owner concludes that customers are willing to pay more for the convenience of not having to haggle.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether Hartwell sold more cars in total last year than in the year before
Whether the prices Hartwell paid at wholesale auctions for the cars it sold were lower last year than the year before
Whether Hartwell's salespeople prefer selling cars at fixed prices
Whether some of Hartwell's customers last year had also bought cars from Hartwell before the switch
Whether no-haggle pricing is more common at new-car dealerships than at used-car dealerships
questions.explanation: Core move: profit per car depends on both selling price and cost, so the useful question is the one that tests whether the profit gain came from the customer side at all. If Hartwell's purchase costs fell, the higher profit could have come from cheaper inventory, not higher prices paid by customers, weakening the argument; if costs held steady, the gain must come from what customers paid, supporting it. The tempting trap is A, but the argument concerns profit per car, and total volume does not tell us whether each customer paid more. C concerns staff preferences, not customer behavior.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Customers will pay more to avoid haggling.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After Hartwell switched to fixed no-haggle prices, its average profit per car rose 8 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Profit per car = what the customer pays minus what the car cost the dealer. The owner assumes the gain came from the customer side. Prephrase: did the dealer's own costs change? If Hartwell bought cars cheaper, profit could rise even if customers paid the same. It's like a bakery saying 'customers love our new recipe' because profit per loaf went up, when flour just got cheaper.

choices.note: Trap. The argument is about profit per car, not total sales. Selling more or fewer cars doesn't tell you whether each buyer paid more.

CORRECT. If auction prices dropped, cheaper inventory could explain the higher profit, and the argument weakens. If costs held steady, the gain must come from what customers paid, and the argument gets stronger.
What salespeople like isn't the question. The conclusion is about what customers are willing to pay.
Repeat customers don't help you sort out whether the profit came from higher prices or lower costs. Doesn't bear on the gap.
Other dealerships' habits are irrelevant to why Hartwell's profit rose.

questions.stimulus: Last spring the Orrin Public Library extended its weekday closing time from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. Over the next six months, library card applications rose by 40 percent compared with the same months a year earlier. Admittedly, a large apartment complex near the library opened during that period, but applications from the complex's residents account for only a small share of the increase. The library's director concludes that the extended hours attracted many residents who previously had been unable to visit the library.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether residents of the new apartment complex tend to visit the library mainly in the evening
Whether the extended hours significantly raised the library's operating costs
Whether the library's evening visitors borrow more books per visit than its daytime visitors do
Whether the library had ever extended its hours on a previous occasion
Whether most of the additional card applications were submitted during the newly added evening hours
questions.explanation: Core move: find the question whose two possible answers point in opposite directions on the claimed mechanism. If most new applications came in after 6 p.m., the extended hours plausibly drew new users; if most came in during the old daytime hours, those applicants could have visited before, and the director's explanation weakens. The strongest trap is A, which revisits the concession, but the argument has already set the complex aside as accounting for only a small share, so its residents' habits cannot decide the issue. C sounds relevant because it compares evening and daytime visitors, but borrowing habits say nothing about who newly applied for cards.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The extended evening hours drew in many residents who couldn't visit the library before.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After hours went to 9 p.m., card applications rose 40 percent; the new apartment complex accounts for only a small share of the increase.

breakdown.analysis: The director claims a specific mechanism: people who couldn't come before 6 p.m. now come in the evening. The simplest way to test that is to ask when the new applications came in. Prephrase: were the new cards signed up for after 6 p.m.? If they were all signed up for at 2 p.m., those people could have come before, and the hours didn't matter. It's like a store crediting its new Sunday hours for a sales jump: check whether the extra sales happened on Sundays.

choices.note: The strongest trap. It goes back to the apartment complex, but the argument already set that aside as only a small share. Its residents' habits can't decide the issue either way.
Cost is about whether the change was worth it, not about why applications rose. Irrelevant.
Sounds relevant because it compares evening and daytime visitors. But borrowing habits say nothing about who newly applied for a card.
Library history doesn't tell you whether this extension caused this increase.

CORRECT. If most new applications came in during the new evening hours, the director's story looks right. If most came in during the old daytime hours, those people could have visited before, and the explanation falls apart.

questions.stimulus: Over the past three years, homes within two kilometers of the Kesby wind farm sold for 6 percent less, on average, than homes farther away in the same county. Opponents of a proposed second wind farm cite this as proof that turbines depress nearby home values. The Kesby farm's operator objects that the homes nearest the farm are, on average, older and smaller. Even so, the opponents are right: when nearby homes are compared only with farther homes of similar age and size, a gap of about 4 percent remains.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether residents living near the Kesby wind farm frequently complain about noise from its turbines
Whether the proposed second wind farm would be located closer to homes than the Kesby farm is
Whether, over the past three years, homes near the Kesby farm sold for less than homes of similar age and size farther away in the county
Whether, in the years before the Kesby farm was built, homes on the land near its site sold for less than similar homes elsewhere in the county
Whether homes near the Kesby farm are, on average, older and smaller than homes farther away
questions.explanation: Core move: the argument controls for age and size but never shows the gap appeared after the turbines arrived, so the key question is the pre-existing base rate. If nearby homes already sold for less before the farm existed, the 4 percent gap reflects something about the location and the argument collapses; if they sold at par, the turbines become the likely cause. The near-miss trap is C, which differs from D only in its time frame: the past three years fall after the farm was built, and the stimulus already answers that question with the 4 percent figure, so knowing it adds nothing. A only cuts one way (complaints would support the conclusion, but their absence would not undermine it, since turbines could depress prices for visual reasons), B bears on the proposed farm rather than this argument, and E is already conceded in the stimulus.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Wind turbines lower the value of nearby homes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Homes within 2 km of Kesby sold for 6 percent less than farther homes; even comparing homes of similar age and size, a 4 percent gap remains.

breakdown.analysis: The opponents fixed one problem (age and size) but never showed the gap showed up after the turbines did. Maybe that land was always cheaper. Prephrase: did those homes sell for less before the farm was built? It's like saying a new highway ruined a neighborhood's property values without checking whether the neighborhood was cheap before the highway. If the gap already existed, the turbines didn't cause it.

choices.note: Only cuts one way. Noise complaints would support the conclusion, but no complaints wouldn't hurt it, since turbines could lower prices just by how they look. A good evaluate answer should matter both ways.
This is about the proposed second farm, not about whether Kesby lowered home values. Wrong target.
Near-miss trap. It looks like D, but it asks about the past three years, which is after the farm was built. The stimulus already answers this with the 4 percent gap. Knowing it again adds nothing.

CORRECT. If nearby homes sold for less before the farm existed, the gap is about the location, and the argument collapses. If they sold at the same price as similar homes, the turbines become the likely cause.
Already conceded in the stimulus. The operator said it and the argument controlled for it. Nothing to learn here.

questions.stimulus: Every glaze stocked by the Harrowgate Pottery Cooperative has been certified food-safe. Marisol, a cooperative member, glazed her new set of soup bowls using only glazes she bought from the cooperative's stock. Marisol also owns several glazes that she bought from other suppliers, and at least one of those glazes has not been certified food-safe. She uses the glazes from other suppliers mainly on decorative tiles.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: None of the glazes Marisol bought from other suppliers has been certified food-safe.
Every certified food-safe glaze that Marisol owns was bought from the cooperative.
Marisol's new soup bowls were glazed only with glazes that have been certified food-safe.
Marisol has never applied an uncertified glaze to anything other than decorative tiles.
Some of the glazes stocked by the cooperative are unsuitable for decorative tiles.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine two facts directly. The bowls used only cooperative glazes, and every cooperative glaze is certified food-safe, so every glaze on the bowls is certified (C). The tempting trap is A, because the stimulus mentions uncertified glazes from other suppliers; but it says only that at least one of them is uncertified, so 'none' is far too strong. B reverses the relationship: all cooperative glazes are certified, but certified glazes could also come from elsewhere, and D overreads 'mainly.'

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every glaze the cooperative stocks is certified food-safe; 2. Marisol glazed her soup bowls only with glazes from the cooperative; 3. She owns other-supplier glazes, and at least one of them is uncertified; 4. She uses the other-supplier glazes mainly on tiles.

breakdown.analysis: Chain facts 1 and 2. Bowls → only co-op glazes. Co-op glaze → certified. So every glaze on the bowls is certified. That's the whole question. It's like: everything sold at this store is organic, and I only bought my dinner ingredients there, so my dinner ingredients are organic.

choices.note: Trap. The stimulus says at least one outside glaze is uncertified. That's 'some,' not 'none.' Others could easily be certified. Watch the jump from 'at least one' to 'all.'
Reversal. All co-op glazes are certified, but that doesn't mean all certified glazes come from the co-op. Some of her outside glazes could be certified too.
CORRECT. The bowls used only co-op glazes, and every co-op glaze is certified food-safe. Put them together and every glaze on the bowls is certified.
Overreads 'mainly.' She uses outside glazes mainly on tiles, which leaves room for other uses. And 'never' is far too strong.
Nothing in the stimulus says anything about which glazes work on tiles. Made up.

questions.stimulus: Under Velmarra's maritime salvage code, a crew that assists a vessel may claim a salvage reward only if the assisted vessel was in genuine peril and the assistance was voluntary rather than owed under a contract. Velmarran courts have found genuine peril in nearly every reported case in which a vessel lost engine power in open water. Last month the fishing trawler Ostrander lost engine power in open water, and the tug Brisa, which had no agreement with the Ostrander's owners, towed it to port.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The Brisa's crew is entitled under the code to a salvage reward for towing the Ostrander.
Any vessel that loses engine power in open water is in genuine peril under Velmarra's code.
Had the Brisa been under contract with the Ostrander's owners, the Ostrander would not have been in genuine peril.
Most salvage claims brought in Velmarran courts involve vessels that lost engine power.
A Velmarran court would probably find that the Ostrander was in genuine peril after it lost engine power.
questions.explanation: Core move: apply a strong-but-not-universal pattern ('nearly every reported case') to a matching instance, which yields a 'probably' conclusion (E). The tempting trap is A: the Brisa appears to meet both listed conditions, but the code states them only as necessary ('only if'), not as sufficient, so nothing establishes entitlement. B turns 'nearly every' into 'any', C invents a link between contracts and peril, and D draws a statistic about all claims from data about one kind of case.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. A crew can claim salvage only if the vessel was in genuine peril AND the help was voluntary, not owed by contract; 2. Courts have found genuine peril in nearly every reported case where a vessel lost engine power in open water; 3. The Ostrander lost engine power in open water; 4. The Brisa, with no agreement, towed it to port.

breakdown.analysis: Fact 2 is a strong pattern, and fact 3 fits it exactly. 'Nearly every' gets you a 'probably,' not a 'definitely.' Also notice the code's conditions are necessary ('only if'), not sufficient. Reward → peril AND voluntary. Meeting both doesn't guarantee a reward. It's like 'you can play varsity only if you pass your classes': passing doesn't put you on the team.

choices.note: Trap. The Brisa seems to meet both conditions, but the code only says you need them, not that they're enough. 'Only if' gives a requirement, not a guarantee.
Too strong. 'Nearly every reported case' isn't 'any vessel.' Courts found exceptions, or at least the stimulus leaves room for them.
Made-up link. A contract affects whether the help was voluntary, not whether the boat was in danger. Peril and contracts are separate conditions.
Wrong statistic. We know what courts found in engine-loss cases, not what share of all salvage claims involve engine loss.

CORRECT. Courts found peril in nearly every reported engine-loss-in-open-water case, and the Ostrander is exactly that kind of case. So a court would probably find peril. 'Probably' matches 'nearly every.'

questions.stimulus: At Pellridge Mountain resort, every trail rated expert is closed on any day the avalanche risk is rated high. No trail is groomed on a day when it is closed. Trails rated intermediate or beginner are closed only at the discretion of the ski patrol. The Corniche is an expert trail, and the Larch Run, an intermediate trail, is groomed on every day the resort operates. Today, the avalanche risk at Pellridge is rated high.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: The Corniche is groomed today.
The Larch Run is closed today.
Some trail at Pellridge that is not rated expert is closed today.
The Corniche was groomed yesterday.
Every trail at Pellridge, including the Corniche, is groomed tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Core move: chain three statements: high risk today, so the expert Corniche is closed today, so it is not groomed today; A therefore cannot be true. The tempting trap is B: if the resort operates today, the Larch Run is groomed and so cannot be closed, but nothing says the resort is operating today, so B could be true. C is allowed by the patrol's discretion, and D and E concern other days, when the risk may not be high.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Expert trail → closed on any high-risk day; 2. Closed → not groomed that day; 3. Intermediate and beginner trails close only at the ski patrol's discretion; 4. The Corniche is expert; the Larch Run (intermediate) is groomed every day the resort operates; 5. Today the risk is high.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. High risk today → Corniche (expert) closed today → Corniche not groomed today. So 'the Corniche is groomed today' is impossible. For a must-be-false question, you want the one answer the facts kill. Everything else just needs to be possible.

choices.note: CORRECT. High risk today means every expert trail is closed today, and a closed trail isn't groomed. The Corniche is expert, so it can't be groomed today.

Trap. If the resort operates today, the Larch Run is groomed and so can't be closed. But nothing says the resort is open today. If it's not operating, the Larch Run could be closed. So B could be true.
Could be true. The patrol can close intermediate or beginner trails whenever it chooses.
Yesterday's risk level isn't given. If it wasn't high, the Corniche could have been open and groomed.
Tomorrow's risk isn't given either. If it drops, every trail could be groomed. Possible, so not the answer.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, rural clinics in the Dunmere district that adopted a telehealth triage system saw average patient wait times fall by about a third, and district officials credit the system for the decline. However, every Dunmere clinic that adopted the system did so under a state grant that also funded an additional full-time nurse. Among Dunmere clinics that hired an additional nurse without adopting the system, average wait times also fell by about a third, while at clinics that did neither, wait times were unchanged. Admittedly, the system has reduced the after-hours calls that physicians must answer.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Telehealth triage systems do not reduce patient wait times at rural clinics.
Hiring an additional full-time nurse is the most cost-effective way for a rural clinic to reduce wait times.
The triage system has benefited Dunmere's physicians more than it has benefited their patients.
The evidence cited does not show that the triage system, rather than the added nurse, is responsible for shorter waits at the clinics that adopted it.
Had the adopting clinics used the triage system without hiring an additional nurse, their wait times would not have fallen.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine three facts (adopters also added a nurse; nurse-only clinics improved just as much; clinics that did neither did not improve) to see that the cause is confounded, which supports only the modest, indirect D. The most tempting trap is E, which reads as the natural lesson of the nurse-only comparison, but it is a confident counterfactual; the data are consistent with the system also cutting waits on its own. A is the same overreach stated generally, which the evidence does not show. C turns the concession into an unsupported comparison, and B brings in cost, which the stimulus never discusses.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Clinics that adopted telehealth triage saw waits fall about a third; officials credit the system; 2. Every adopting clinic also got a grant-funded extra nurse; 3. Clinics that added a nurse without the system also saw waits fall about a third; 4. Clinics that did neither saw no change; 5. The system has cut physicians' after-hours calls.

breakdown.analysis: Every clinic with the system also got a nurse, and the nurse alone produced the same drop. So you can't tell whether the system did anything. That's a confound. It doesn't prove the system is useless; it just means this evidence can't credit it. It's like taking vitamins and starting to exercise the same week, then crediting the vitamins for feeling better. Supported-answer questions reward the modest claim.

choices.note: Too strong. The evidence can't credit the system, but it also doesn't show the system does nothing. Lack of proof isn't proof of no effect.
Cost-effectiveness never comes up. We don't know what the nurse or the system costs.
Turns the concession into a comparison. We know the system cut physicians' after-hours calls, but nothing shows it helped them more than it helped patients.

CORRECT. The adopting clinics got the nurse too, and nurse-only clinics improved just as much. So the evidence can't separate the system's effect from the nurse's. That's all D claims, and the facts fully back it.

The most tempting trap. It sounds like the natural lesson, but it's a confident 'what would have happened.' The system might also cut waits by itself; the data just can't tell. You can't pick an answer that needs more than the facts give.
