questions.stimulus: Most members of the Calloway Symphony's string section trained at the Wexley Conservatory, and most members of the string section have perfect pitch. Every Wexley-trained member of the orchestra has performed in the orchestra's chamber series. Admittedly, the chamber series is not limited to string players: several wind players have performed in it as well, and only some of those wind players trained at Wexley.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Most members of the string section who have perfect pitch have performed in the chamber series.
At least one member of the orchestra who has perfect pitch has performed in the chamber series.
Some Wexley-trained members of the string section do not have perfect pitch.
Most of the musicians who have performed in the chamber series are members of the string section.
Some member of the string section who has perfect pitch has not performed in the chamber series.
questions.explanation: Core move: 'most + most' within the same group (the string section) guarantees at least one overlap, so some string player is both Wexley-trained and has perfect pitch; the conditional then puts that player in the chamber series, which gives B. The most tempting trap is A, which differs from B by one quantifier: the overlap is guaranteed to be at least one person, not a majority of the perfect-pitch players, and the perfect-pitch players who are not from Wexley might never have performed. C and E could both be false if every Wexley-trained string player has perfect pitch, and if every perfect-pitch string player trained at Wexley. D is unsupported because the number of wind performers is not given.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Most string players trained at Wexley; 2. Most string players have perfect pitch; 3. Every Wexley-trained orchestra member has played in the chamber series; 4. Some wind players have played in the series too, and only some of them trained at Wexley.

breakdown.analysis: Most + most of the same group means at least one overlap. Picture 10 string players: 6 from Wexley, 6 with perfect pitch. They can't all be different people, so at least 2 have both. Then Wexley → chamber series, so that person has played in the series. So at least one perfect-pitch member has played in the series. That's all you get: 'at least one,' not 'most.'

choices.note: The most tempting trap, one quantifier off. The overlap is guaranteed to be at least one person, not most of the perfect-pitch players. The perfect-pitch players who didn't train at Wexley might never have played in the series.
CORRECT. Most string players are Wexley-trained and most have perfect pitch, so at least one string player is both. Every Wexley-trained member has played the chamber series, so that player has too.
Could be false. Maybe every Wexley-trained string player has perfect pitch. Nothing rules that out.
We don't know how many wind players have performed, just 'several.' They could outnumber the string players in the series.
Could be false. If every perfect-pitch string player trained at Wexley, they've all played in the series.

questions.stimulus: Privacy consultant: A business that collects a customer's personal information for a specific purpose should delete that information once it is no longer needed for that purpose. Keeping such information longer serves no legitimate business need, and it exposes the customer to the risk of a data breach with no offsetting benefit. A business that wants to keep such information for some other purpose should ask for the customer's permission.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Corbel Bank should delete the account records of a customer who still has an open loan, because the customer has asked to stop receiving marketing mail.
Tarnwell Outfitters collected customers' shipping addresses solely to deliver orders, so once an order has arrived and its return period has ended, Tarnwell should delete that address.
Pyle Books collects customers' email addresses to send receipts, so it should never use those addresses for any other purpose.
Medline Pharmacy should keep its customers' prescription records indefinitely, since the records might someday be useful for research.
Because data breaches harm customers, Velo Gyms should not collect any personal information from its members.
questions.explanation: Core move: match the principle's trigger (data collected for a purpose, and that purpose fully served) to its result (delete). In B the address was collected only for delivery and returns, both finished, so deletion follows. The tempting trap is C, which sounds privacy-friendly and concerns using data for its original purpose, but the principle is about how long data is kept, not what it may be used for. A deletes data that is still needed for the open loan, D contradicts the principle, and E goes far beyond it.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If a business collected personal info for a specific purpose AND that info is no longer needed for that purpose → delete it. To keep it for another purpose → ask the customer's permission.

breakdown.analysis: Find the answer that meets the trigger (collected for a purpose, purpose finished) and draws the result (delete). Note what the principle is about: how long data is kept, not what it can be used for. The LSAT is ultra specific: an answer about use isn't an answer about keeping.

choices.note: Backwards. The customer still has an open loan, so the records are still needed. And 'stop marketing mail' isn't the purpose that matters.
CORRECT. Tarnwell collected addresses only to deliver orders. Once delivery and the return period are done, the purpose is finished, so the principle says delete.
Trap. It sounds privacy-friendly, but the principle is about holding data too long, not about uses. And 'never' ignores the principle's own option: ask permission for other uses.
Directly against the principle. 'Might someday be useful' is keeping data with no current need and no permission.
Way beyond the principle. It doesn't ban collecting data; it says what to do once the purpose is over.

questions.stimulus: The Ashby town council should not require clay tile roofs on new houses in the town's historic district. The requirement is meant to preserve the district's traditional appearance. But clay tiles cost about three times as much as the composite tiles that builders would otherwise use, and from the street, composite tiles cannot be distinguished from clay.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: Building rules for a historic district should require traditional materials wherever it is technically feasible to use them.
A town council should adopt a building requirement only if most of the affected property owners support it.
When two roofing materials cost the same, a town should require the one that more closely matches traditional construction.
A rule intended to preserve a district's appearance should not mandate a costly material when a much cheaper one gives the public the same appearance.
New houses should be built with whatever roofing material is expected to last the longest.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the principle whose conditions match the argument's premises (the rule's goal is appearance, the cheaper material looks the same, the mandated material costs much more) and whose result is the conclusion (don't mandate it). D does exactly that. The tempting trap is C, which shares the topic of cost and tradition, but its condition (equal cost) is not met here, so it cannot produce the conclusion. A points toward the opposite conclusion, and B and E bring in factors the argument never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ashby shouldn't require clay tile roofs on new houses in the historic district.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule's goal is the district's traditional look; clay costs about three times as much as composite; from the street, composite looks the same as clay.

breakdown.analysis: You want a principle that takes the premises as its 'if' and the conclusion as its 'then.' If a rule is about appearance AND a much cheaper material looks the same → don't require the costly one. It's like a dress code requiring real silk ties when polyester looks identical across the room. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: Points the opposite way. Clay is technically feasible, so this would support requiring it.
New factor. The argument never mentions what property owners want.
Trap. Same topic (cost and tradition), but its condition is equal cost, and here clay costs three times as much. Its condition isn't met, so it can't produce the conclusion.
CORRECT. The rule is about appearance, composite costs far less, and the public sees the same thing. So the principle says don't mandate clay. Premises in, conclusion out.
Durability never comes up in the argument. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Foraging association guideline: A guide who allows a client to eat a wild mushroom that the guide has not personally identified is negligent, regardless of how the mushroom affects the client. A guide's role is to stand between clients and the hazards of misidentification, and that role is abandoned the moment the guide defers to anyone else's judgment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Bram personally identified every mushroom his clients ate during the outing, so Bram was not negligent.
Corrie's client became ill after eating a mushroom on Corrie's outing, so Corrie must not have personally identified that mushroom.
Dagny was negligent, because she misidentified a mushroom on the outing, even though she stopped her client from eating it.
Since Emeric's client correctly identified a chanterelle on her own, Emeric was not negligent in letting her eat it.
Ottilie was negligent, since she let a client eat a puffball that only the client had identified, even though the puffball proved harmless.
questions.explanation: Core move: the guideline gives a sufficient condition for negligence (allowing a client to eat a mushroom the guide did not identify), and E satisfies it exactly; 'regardless of how the mushroom affects the client' makes the harmless outcome irrelevant. The most tempting trap is A, which denies the sufficient condition and concludes no negligence; but the guideline names only one way to be negligent, not the only way, so it is silent on Bram. B reasons backward from a bad outcome to a missing identification, which the guideline never links. C finds negligence on grounds the guideline doesn't address, and D contradicts it.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If a guide lets a client eat a wild mushroom the guide did not personally identify → the guide is negligent, no matter what the mushroom does to the client.

breakdown.analysis: This gives one sufficient condition for negligence. Didn't personally identify AND let client eat → negligent. It doesn't say that's the only way to be negligent, and it says the outcome doesn't matter. Find the answer where the guide let a client eat something only someone else identified, and called it negligent.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. Bram avoided the one listed way to be negligent, but the guideline doesn't say it's the only way. Denying the trigger doesn't get you 'not negligent.' The rule is silent here.
Reasons backward from a bad outcome. Illness doesn't prove the guide skipped identification; even correctly identified mushrooms might make someone sick. The guideline never links them.
Different grounds. Dagny stopped the client from eating, so the trigger isn't met. Misidentifying alone isn't covered by the guideline.
Contradicts it. The guide deferred to the client's ID, and the guideline says that's negligent no matter how accurate the client was.
CORRECT. Ottilie let a client eat a puffball only the client had identified. That's the trigger. 'Regardless of how the mushroom affects the client' makes 'harmless' irrelevant. Negligent.

questions.stimulus: The Halvard Survey Office should not yet release its revised nautical chart of Selden Bay. Admittedly, the revision corrects several depth errors in the current chart, errors that harbor pilots have complained about for years. But the revision was compiled entirely from the office's own sonar soundings, and no one outside the office has checked either those soundings or the chart drawn from them. Releasing the revision now would therefore be premature, however welcome its corrections.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: A survey office should release a chart revision only after someone independent of the office has checked it, even if the revision corrects errors that mariners have long complained about.
A survey office should release any chart revision that has been checked by someone independent of the office.
A chart revision that corrects errors mariners have complained about should be released as soon as it is completed.
A survey office should compile charts from its own soundings only when soundings from independent sources are unavailable.
A chart revision should be released only if it corrects errors that make the current chart hazardous to mariners.
questions.explanation: Core move: to justify NOT releasing, the principle must make independent checking a necessary condition for release; the chart fails that condition, so release is ruled out, and A's 'even if' clause also neutralizes the concession. The most tempting trap is B, which uses the right idea backward: it makes independent checking sufficient for release, so it says nothing about an unchecked chart. E is the subtler trap: it states a necessary condition that this revision arguably satisfies (it corrects depth errors), and meeting a necessary condition does not require or forbid release. D concerns how charts are compiled, not whether this one may be released, and C points toward the opposite conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Halvard office shouldn't release its revised Selden Bay chart yet.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The revision fixes long-complained-about depth errors; but it's built entirely from the office's own soundings, and no one outside the office has checked them or the chart.

breakdown.analysis: To justify NOT releasing, you need independent checking to be required for release. Release → independently checked. Contrapositive: not checked → don't release. The chart isn't checked, so don't release. Bonus points if the principle also deals with the concession (the corrections are welcome). Watch for answers that flip necessary and sufficient.

choices.note: CORRECT. Independent checking is required for release, and this chart hasn't had it, so no release. The 'even if' clause handles the concession about long-complained-about errors.
The most tempting trap. Right idea, wrong direction. It makes checking enough to release, which says nothing about a chart nobody has checked.
Points the other way. This would say release now.
About how charts get compiled, not whether this one can be released. Doesn't reach the conclusion.
Subtle trap. It's a necessary condition the chart arguably meets (it fixes depth errors). Meeting a requirement doesn't forbid release, so this can't justify holding it back.

questions.stimulus: Orchestra administrator: Our new attendance rule is this: a musician who misses the dress rehearsal for a concert must not be permitted to play in that concert, unless the absence resulted from an emergency and the musician notified the personnel manager before the rehearsal began. Admittedly, the rule will occasionally keep a well-prepared musician off the stage. But the dress rehearsal is the only time the full ensemble tests the hall's acoustics together, and a rule with few exceptions is hard to abuse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the rule stated by the administrator?
choices: Since Halvor attended the dress rehearsal, the rule requires that he be permitted to play in the concert.

Because Rosalind's absence from the dress rehearsal resulted from a genuine emergency, the rule does not require that she be kept out of the concert, even though she first contacted the personnel manager the following day.

Ines missed the dress rehearsal, but because a burst pipe flooded her apartment that morning and she phoned the personnel manager an hour before the rehearsal, the rule does not require that she be kept out of the concert.
Tomas told the personnel manager a week in advance that he would miss the dress rehearsal to attend a friend's wedding, so the rule allows him to play in the concert.
Because Yuki's absence from the dress rehearsal resulted from an emergency that she reported to the personnel manager beforehand, the rule requires that she be permitted to play in the concert.
questions.explanation: Core move: 'X must not play unless E1 and E2' means that if either exception condition fails, the musician is barred; if both hold, the rule simply stops requiring a bar and does not grant a right to play. C triggers the exception precisely (a real emergency AND notice before the rehearsal) and draws only the limited conclusion that the rule does not require exclusion. The most tempting trap is E: it describes the same exception-triggering facts but concludes that the rule REQUIRES that Yuki be allowed to play, turning an exception into a guarantee the rule never gives (A makes the same mistake for a musician who attended). B and D each satisfy only one of the two exception conditions (an emergency but late notice; early notice but no emergency), so the rule actually requires barring those musicians.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If a musician misses the dress rehearsal → can't play, unless (emergency AND told the personnel manager before rehearsal). Missed AND (no emergency OR no advance notice) → barred.

breakdown.analysis: 'Must not play unless X' means: without X, you're barred. With X, the rule just stops requiring a bar; it doesn't promise you a seat. So the right answer meets both exception conditions and only concludes the rule doesn't require exclusion. It's like 'no dessert unless you finish dinner': finishing dinner doesn't guarantee dessert.

choices.note: Turns the rule into a guarantee. The rule only says who must be barred. Attending doesn't mean the rule requires that Halvor play.
Only one of two conditions. It was an emergency, but she called the next day. The exception needs notice before the rehearsal, so the rule requires barring her.
CORRECT. A burst pipe is an emergency, and she called before rehearsal. Both exception conditions are met, and the answer draws only the limited conclusion: the rule doesn't require keeping her out.
Only one of two conditions. Advance notice, yes, but a friend's wedding isn't an emergency. The rule bars Tomas.
The most tempting trap. Same facts as C, but it says the rule requires she be allowed to play. An exception just lifts the ban; it doesn't create a right.

questions.stimulus: Several deadly mushroom species share certain visible features. If a mushroom brought to the Brackenfield market has white gills and a ring on its stem, the market's inspector will not allow it to be sold. The mushroom that Pell brought to the market this morning has white gills and a ring on its stem. So the inspector will not allow Pell's mushroom to be sold.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: If a kiln reaches cone 10, the stoneware fired in it will vitrify. The stoneware Hollis fired yesterday vitrified. So Hollis's kiln must have reached cone 10.
If a ski run is both steep and icy, the patrol will close it. The Ridgeback run is not being closed. So the Ridgeback run must not be both steep and icy.
If a ship flies a foreign flag and carries cargo, it must pay the harbor fee. The Marlow flies a foreign flag. So the Marlow must pay the harbor fee.

If an audition recording is both unedited and under ten minutes long, the committee will not reject it unheard. Aster's recording is unedited and under ten minutes long. So the committee will not reject Aster's recording unheard.
Most mushrooms with white gills are unsafe to eat. The mushroom Pell found has white gills. So Pell's mushroom is probably unsafe to eat.
questions.explanation: Core move: identify the pattern: if A and B, then not C; this case has A and B; so not C. D matches it exactly, including both conditions and the negative result. The most tempting trap is C, which looks similar but concludes after only one of the two required conditions is met (we don't know the Marlow carries cargo). B is a valid argument with a different pattern (it infers backward from a result that did not happen), A infers the condition from the result, and E reasons from 'most' to 'probably' rather than from a conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The inspector won't let Pell's mushroom be sold.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: White gills AND a ring → inspector won't allow sale; Pell's mushroom has white gills and a ring.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: If A and B, then not C; this case has A and B; so not C.

breakdown.analysis: This is a plain, valid conditional: both conditions met, so the negative result follows. The first sentence about deadly species is just background. Match three things: two conditions, both confirmed, and a 'won't' conclusion. Don't get distracted by answers that share the mushroom topic; parallel questions are about structure, not subject.

choices.note: Backwards. It goes from the result (vitrified) to the condition (cone 10). The stimulus goes from the conditions to the result. That's a different, flawed pattern.
Valid, but a different pattern. It uses the contrapositive: result didn't happen, so the conditions weren't both met. The stimulus goes forward.
The most tempting trap. Same two-condition shape, but only one condition is confirmed. We don't know the Marlow carries cargo. The stimulus confirms both.
CORRECT. Two conditions (unedited, under ten minutes) → won't be rejected unheard. Aster's has both. So it won't be rejected unheard. Two conditions, both met, negative result. Exact match.
Uses 'most' and 'probably,' not a conditional rule. Same topic, different structure. It even reuses Pell to tempt you.

questions.stimulus: Roofing contractor: Salt spray and winter gales in the coastal town of Brennock destroy most roofing materials within a few decades. A roof in Brennock can last fifty years only if it is made of slate or of copper. The new roof on Brennock's public library is made of slate. Therefore, the library's new roof will last fifty years.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: A pottery student can enter the advanced studio only if she has completed either the wheel course or the handbuilding course. Rhea has completed the wheel course. Therefore, Rhea can enter the advanced studio.
If a roof is made of slate, it will last fifty years. The roof on Brennock's museum is not made of slate. Therefore, the museum's roof will not last fifty years.
A map can be certified only if it has been checked in the field. This map has not been checked in the field. Therefore, this map cannot be certified.
A clinic can receive the rural health grant only if it serves a rural county. The Ferris clinic received the grant. Therefore, the Ferris clinic serves a rural county.
Most roofs made of slate last fifty years. The library's new roof is made of slate. Therefore, the library's new roof will certainly last fifty years.
questions.explanation: Core move: the argument treats a necessary condition ('only if slate or copper') as sufficient, and A makes the same error with the same 'either/or' necessary condition. The most tempting trap is B, which shares the topic and vocabulary, but its flaw is different: it assumes that failing a sufficient condition guarantees failure. C and D are valid uses of 'only if' (C denies the necessary condition; D infers the necessary condition from the outcome). E's error is overstating a 'most' statement, not confusing necessary and sufficient conditions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The library's slate roof will last fifty years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A Brennock roof lasts fifty years only if it's slate or copper; the library roof is slate.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X only if A or B; this case has A; so X. (Treats a necessary condition as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' gives a requirement. Lasts 50 years → slate OR copper. Being slate doesn't guarantee 50 years; it just means you're eligible. It's like saying 'you can win the lottery only if you buy a ticket; I bought one, so I'll win.' Find the answer that makes the same necessary-as-sufficient error, ideally with an either/or requirement.

choices.note: CORRECT. Entering requires the wheel OR handbuilding course. Rhea completed one, so the argument says she can enter. That treats the requirement as a guarantee, the exact same flaw, with the same either/or shape.

The most tempting trap. Same topic, but a different flaw. It takes a sufficient condition (slate → 50 years) and assumes failing it means failing the result. That's denying the condition, not mixing up necessary and sufficient.
Valid. Certified → checked. Not checked → not certified. That's the contrapositive. No flaw here.
Valid. Grant → rural. Got the grant, so rural. That's using the rule in the right direction.
Different flaw. It turns 'most' into 'certainly.' No necessary/sufficient confusion.

questions.stimulus: The Linwood Historical Archive holds several thousand maps, most of them donated by the families of nineteenth-century surveyors. Every map in the archive that was drawn before 1850 was colored by hand. None of the hand-colored maps in the archive has been digitized. So none of the archive's pre-1850 maps has been digitized.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every ski instructor at Halden Peak has first-aid training. None of the resort's lift operators is a ski instructor. So none of the resort's lift operators has first-aid training.
Most of the Ardgour clinic's nurses speak Gaelic. None of the clinic's Gaelic speakers works the night shift. So most of the clinic's nurses do not work the night shift.
Every pot fired in the studio's wood kiln has an ash glaze. None of the studio's ash-glazed pots has been sold. So none of the pots fired in the studio's wood kiln has been sold.
Every cellist in the Ardmore Orchestra owns a carbon-fiber bow. Every orchestra member who owns a carbon-fiber bow tours abroad. So every cellist in the orchestra tours abroad.
No vessel in the Corran fleet has a steel hull. Every vessel with a steel hull must be inspected yearly. So no vessel in the Corran fleet must be inspected yearly.
questions.explanation: Core move: match a quantified chain: all A are B; no B is C; therefore no A is C (valid). C has the identical structure and quantifiers. The most tempting trap is B, which is also valid and chains in the same direction, but it begins with 'most' and so concludes with 'most,' which is a different pattern. D is a valid all-all chain with a positive conclusion, while A and E are invalid chains that negate the wrong term.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the archive's pre-1850 maps has been digitized.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every pre-1850 map was hand-colored; no hand-colored map has been digitized.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; no B is C; so no A is C.

breakdown.analysis: Valid chain: pre-1850 → hand-colored → not digitized. Match the quantifiers in order: 'all,' then 'none,' then 'none.' The first sentence about donations is filler. Check each answer's quantifiers and which term gets negated.

choices.note: Invalid. All A are B; no C is A; so no C is B. It negates the wrong term. Lift operators could have first-aid training without being instructors.
The most tempting trap. It's valid and chains the same way, but it starts with 'most' and ends with 'most.' Different quantifiers, different pattern.
CORRECT. Every wood-kiln pot has an ash glaze; no ash-glazed pot has sold; so no wood-kiln pot has sold. All A are B, no B is C, so no A is C. Exact match.
Valid, but all-all with a positive conclusion. The stimulus has a 'none' link and a negative conclusion.
Invalid. It says no Corran vessel is steel, and steel ones must be inspected, so no Corran vessel must be. Inspection could be required for other reasons. Negates the wrong term.

questions.stimulus: Corvane Peak resort trains all of its staff in basic first aid, but certification in avalanche rescue is optional. Most of the ski instructors at Corvane Peak are certified in avalanche rescue. Moreover, most of the Corvane Peak staff members who hold that certification work on the ski patrol. Therefore, most of Corvane Peak's ski instructors work on the ski patrol.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the musicians in the Hollin Symphony live in the city, and most of the Hollin Symphony's musicians teach privately. Therefore, at least some of the Hollin Symphony's musicians both live in the city and teach privately.
Every rural clinic in Tarrow County has an on-site pharmacy, and most clinics with an on-site pharmacy stay open on weekends. Therefore, most of Tarrow County's rural clinics stay open on weekends.
Most of the maps in the Pell collection are engraved, and every engraved map in the Pell collection is signed. Therefore, most of the maps in the Pell collection are signed.
Most of the mushrooms the foraging club found were edible, and most of the club's edible finds were boletes. Therefore, most of the boletes the club found were edible.

Most members of the Wrenfield potters' guild sell at the summer craft fair, and most of the potters who sell at that fair use local clay. Therefore, most members of the Wrenfield guild use local clay.
questions.explanation: Core move: the flaw is chaining two 'most' statements (most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C), which fails because the A's that are B may fall among the B's that are not C. E repeats exactly that chain. The strongest trap is B, which is also flawed, but its first premise is 'every' rather than 'most', so it differs by one quantifier and is a different pattern. A (most + most over the same group gives some overlap) and C (most + all gives most) are valid, which makes them attractive to anyone who matches only surface quantifiers, and D's conclusion reverses the terms instead of chaining them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Corvane Peak ski instructors work on the ski patrol.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most instructors hold avalanche certification; most certified staff work on the patrol.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C. (Flawed.)

breakdown.analysis: Chaining two 'most' statements fails. Imagine 100 certified staff: 60 on patrol, 40 not. If there are 10 instructors and 8 are certified, those 8 could all be among the 40 non-patrol people. So most instructors might not be on the patrol. Find the answer that chains most + most in the same order.

choices.note: Valid, so it can't match a flaw. Most + most of the same group guarantees at least some overlap. Tempting if you only count 'most's.
The strongest trap. It's flawed, but the first premise is 'every,' not 'most.' One quantifier off makes it a different pattern.
Valid. Most are engraved and every engraved one is signed, so most are signed. Most + all works.
Different move. It doesn't chain to a new group; it flips the terms of a 'most' statement (most edible finds were boletes → most boletes were edible). A reversal, not a chain.
CORRECT. Most guild members sell at the fair; most fair sellers use local clay; so most guild members use local clay. Most A are B, most B are C, so most A are C. Same flaw, same order.

questions.stimulus: Under the Varnholt Data Code, any mobile app that collects users' location data must obtain each user's explicit consent, and any app that obtains explicit consent must keep a consent log open to regulators. Regulators have confirmed that the Trailmark hiking app keeps such a log. So Trailmark must have obtained explicit consent from its users, and it must therefore be collecting their location data.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Under the Varnholt Data Code, any app that collects health data must encrypt it, and any app that encrypts user data must submit to an annual audit. The Pulsewise app collects health data. So Pulsewise must encrypt that data, and it must therefore submit to an annual audit.

Under Fenwick Studio's rules, any glaze containing copper must be fired in the reduction kiln, and any glaze fired in the reduction kiln must be tested for leaching. The studio's new crimson glaze has been tested for leaching. So it must have been fired in the reduction kiln, and it must therefore contain copper.

Under the Varnholt Data Code, any app that shares user data with advertisers must disclose that practice, and any app that discloses it must offer an opt-out. Trailmark does not share user data with advertisers. So it need not disclose any such practice, and it therefore need not offer an opt-out.

Under the Varnholt Data Code, any app that stores biometric data must appoint a privacy officer, and any app that appoints a privacy officer must file an annual report. The Gripline app has filed no annual report. So it has not appointed a privacy officer, and it therefore does not store biometric data.

Under Pinehollow's building code, any roof shingled with cedar must be treated with fire retardant, and any roof in the Pinehollow fire zone must be treated with fire retardant. The Aldane house is in the fire zone. So its roof must be treated with fire retardant, and it must therefore be shingled with cedar.
questions.explanation: Core move: diagram the stimulus as A->B, B->C; C is true; therefore B (an intermediate conclusion that affirms the consequent), therefore A (affirming the consequent again). B reproduces both reversed steps link for link, despite its unrelated topic. The most tempting trap is E, which copies the wording and two-step shape but has one link reversed (the fire-zone premise runs C->B, not B->C), so its first inference is valid and only its second is flawed; that is a different pattern. A, C and D deliberately share the stimulus's data-privacy vocabulary, but A is a valid forward chain, D is a valid contrapositive chain, and C commits a different flaw (denying the antecedent).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Trailmark got explicit consent, so it must be collecting location data.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Collects location → needs consent; has consent → keeps a log; Trailmark keeps a log.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B, B → C; C is true; so B; so A. (Affirms the consequent twice.)

breakdown.analysis: The rules run forward: location → consent → log. The argument runs backward twice: log, so consent, so location. Each step reverses a conditional. It's like saying: everyone who runs a marathon trains, and everyone who trains is tired; I'm tired, so I trained, so I ran a marathon. Ignore the topic; several answers reuse the privacy wording to trick you.

choices.note: Valid forward chain. Health data → encrypt → audit; Pulsewise collects health data, so encrypt, so audit. Right direction. Same topic, but no flaw.
CORRECT. Copper → reduction kiln → leaching test. The glaze was tested, so the argument says it was fired in reduction, so it has copper. Backward twice, link for link. Different topic, same flaw.
Different flaw. It denies the first condition and concludes the rest fails: doesn't share, so needn't disclose, so needn't offer opt-out. That's denying the antecedent, not affirming the consequent.
Valid. No report → no officer → no biometric data. That's the contrapositive chain, correctly done.

The most tempting trap. It looks like the stimulus, but the fire-zone rule runs into the same result (fire zone → retardant), so its first step is valid. Only the second step reverses. One flaw instead of two is a different pattern.

questions.stimulus: Fluoride varnish should be offered to every child at the Brightwater school dental screenings. The varnish takes less than a minute to apply, and the hygienists who already staff the screenings can apply it without any additional training. Furthermore, in a two-year trial at three Brightwater schools, children who received the varnish developed far fewer cavities than children who did not.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Applying fluoride varnish takes little time and requires no additional training for the screening hygienists.
Every child at the Brightwater school dental screenings should be offered fluoride varnish.
Children who received fluoride varnish in a two-year trial developed far fewer cavities than children who did not.
The hygienists who staff the Brightwater screenings are trained to perform most dental procedures.
Fluoride varnish is the most effective available means of preventing cavities in children.
questions.explanation: Core move: identifying a conclusion stated in the first sentence, with the support following it. Everything after the first sentence gives reasons (speed, no extra training, trial results) for offering the varnish, so B is the conclusion. The tempting trap is C, the most striking piece of evidence; it is tempting because it sounds like a finding, but it is offered to support the recommendation, not drawn from it. A is also a premise, D distorts it, and E is far stronger than anything stated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every child at the Brightwater screenings should be offered fluoride varnish.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It takes under a minute; current hygienists can apply it without extra training; a two-year trial found far fewer cavities with it.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion is the first sentence. Everything after it answers 'why should we?': it's quick, it's easy, and it works. Test: does the recommendation support the trial result, or does the trial result support the recommendation? The second. So the recommendation is the conclusion.

choices.note: A premise. Speed and no extra training are reasons to offer the varnish, not the point being argued.
CORRECT. This is the first sentence, restated. Every other sentence is a reason for it.
The tempting trap. It's the most striking fact and sounds like a finding. But it's offered to support the recommendation, so it's a premise.
Distorts a premise. The stimulus says hygienists need no extra training for the varnish, not that they can do most procedures.
Way too strong. Nothing compares varnish to every other way of preventing cavities.

questions.stimulus: Some members of the Ashby town council argue that the town no longer needs a local newspaper, since residents can follow council business on the council’s own website. Nonetheless, the Ashby Herald should keep the town’s legal-notice contract, which is the paper’s main source of steady income. The council’s website reports only what the council chooses to publish, whereas Herald reporters have twice uncovered budget errors that the council’s own summaries omitted. A town that relies solely on its government’s account of itself has no independent check on that government.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the council’s website reports only what the council chooses to publish?
choices: It is the argument’s main conclusion.
It is a view the argument attributes to some council members and then rejects.
It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim that Herald reporters have uncovered budget errors.
It is offered as support for the claim that the Herald should keep the town’s legal-notice contract.
It is a concession that the council’s website provides residents with some useful information.
questions.explanation: Core move: finding a conclusion placed mid-paragraph after an opposing view, then classifying a claim relative to it. The main conclusion is the second sentence (the Herald should keep the contract); the claim about the website is one of the reasons offered for it, so D. The tempting trap is B, because the website is first raised by the council members; but their view is that the town no longer needs a paper, and the claim in question is the author’s own point against them. Nothing in the argument supports the claim (ruling out C), and it is a criticism of the website, not a concession (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ashby Herald should keep the town's legal-notice contract.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The council's website reports only what the council chooses; Herald reporters twice caught budget errors the council's summaries left out; a town that relies only on its government's account has no independent check.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph opens with an opposing view (the council's site makes the paper unnecessary), then 'Nonetheless' flags the author's conclusion. The website claim comes right after and explains why the site isn't enough. So it's a reason for the conclusion. Role questions: find the main conclusion first, then ask what the claim does for it.

choices.note: No. The main conclusion is the 'Nonetheless' sentence about keeping the contract.

The tempting trap, because the council members bring up the website. But their view is that the town doesn't need a paper. The claim that the site reports only what the council chooses is the author's own point against them.
Nothing supports this claim. The budget-errors claim sits beside it as another reason; it doesn't prove the website point.
CORRECT. The website only publishes what the council wants, so it can't replace an independent paper. That's a reason the Herald should keep the contract.
It's a criticism of the website, not a concession. The author isn't granting the website anything here.

questions.stimulus: Many glaciologists hold that the dark bands visible in the Serren Icefield are layers of volcanic ash, since the icefield lies downwind of two active volcanoes. However, the bands are more likely to be dust deposited during unusually dry summers. Chemical analysis of samples from the bands found none of the tiny glass shards that volcanic ash invariably contains, and the spacing of the bands matches the record of drought years kept at the nearby Lisk weather station.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: showing that the evidence cited in support of a rival view is inaccurate
rejecting a view because those who hold it rely on an unrepresentative sample
citing the authority of experts to defend an explanation against an objection
concluding that the bands cannot be volcanic ash because there is no proof that they are
favoring one explanation over another by noting a predicted feature that is absent and an observation that fits
questions.explanation: Core move: describing an argument whose conclusion follows ‘however’ and rejects a stated opposing view. The author prefers the dust explanation because ash would leave glass shards (absent) and because band spacing matches drought years (fits), which is E. The tempting trap is A: the argument does reject the glaciologists’ view, but it never disputes their evidence (the icefield really is downwind of volcanoes); it argues that other evidence outweighs it. D misstates both the strength (‘cannot’ vs ‘more likely’) and the reasoning, since the absence of shards is positive evidence, not mere lack of proof.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The dark bands in the Serren Icefield are more likely dust from dry summers than volcanic ash.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ash always contains tiny glass shards, but samples from the bands had none; the band spacing matches the local record of drought years.

breakdown.analysis: The author picks between two explanations. Two pieces of evidence: something the ash theory predicts is missing (glass shards), and something the dust theory predicts shows up (spacing matches droughts). Note the author never says the glaciologists' fact is false; the icefield really is downwind of volcanoes. It's like ruling out a burglar because nothing's missing, and noticing the mess matches the dog's paw prints.

choices.note: Trap. The argument does reject the glaciologists' view, but it never says their evidence is wrong. It accepts that the icefield is downwind of volcanoes and argues other evidence outweighs that.
choices.example: Example of this method: Critics say the bridge is unsafe because it has cracks. But the inspection they cite was of a different bridge, so their evidence doesn't hold.

choices.note: No sample problem is raised. The author doesn't say the glaciologists studied too few bands or the wrong ones.
choices.example: Example of this method: The survey says students love the new menu, but it only polled the student council, so the view should be rejected.

choices.note: The author argues against the experts, not by relying on them. No authority is cited for the dust view.
choices.example: Example of this method: Some say this painting is a forgery, but three leading museum curators have examined it and say it is genuine.

choices.note: Wrong strength and wrong reasoning. The conclusion is 'more likely,' not 'cannot.' And missing shards is positive evidence against ash, not just a lack of proof.
choices.example: Example of this method: No one has proven the mayor took the bribe, so she must not have taken it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ash would leave glass shards, and there are none (a predicted feature that's absent). The spacing matches drought years (an observation that fits). On that basis the author favors dust over ash.

questions.stimulus: Some chess coaches insist that beginners should memorize opening variations before studying anything else, because many beginners’ games are lost within the first dozen moves. Beginners do lose many games early. Nevertheless, these coaches have the order of instruction backward. Beginners’ early losses rarely result from not knowing named variations; they result from leaving pieces undefended, a habit that tactical puzzles correct far more efficiently than opening study does. Every hour a beginner spends memorizing variations is therefore an hour taken from the very training that would prevent those early losses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: Coaches are mistaken to have beginners memorize opening variations before studying other aspects of the game.
Time that beginners spend memorizing opening variations is time taken from the training that would best prevent their early losses.
Beginners’ early losses are usually caused by leaving pieces undefended rather than by ignorance of opening variations.
Many games played by beginners are lost within the first dozen moves.
Beginners should not study opening variations at any stage of their chess training.
questions.explanation: Core move: separating a mid-paragraph main conclusion from an intermediate conclusion that comes last. ‘These coaches have the order of instruction backward’ is the claim everything else supports, and A restates it. The strongest trap is B, the final sentence flagged by ‘therefore’: it is a conclusion, but it is drawn in order to show the coaches’ ordering is wrong, so it is intermediate. C is a premise supporting B, D is a concession, and E is too strong, since the argument objects only to putting openings first.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Coaches who make beginners memorize openings first have the order of instruction backward.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Beginners' early losses come from undefended pieces, not from not knowing variations; tactical puzzles fix that faster than opening study; so every hour on variations is an hour taken from the training that would prevent early losses.

breakdown.analysis: The structure: opposing view, concession ('Beginners do lose many games early'), then 'Nevertheless' and the main point. The last sentence starts with 'therefore,' but it's a stepping stone: it shows why the coaches' order is backward. Test: does B support A, or A support B? Wasted hours show the order is wrong. So the 'backward' claim is the main conclusion. A last-sentence 'therefore' doesn't automatically mean main conclusion.

choices.note: CORRECT. This restates 'these coaches have the order of instruction backward.' Everything else in the argument supports it.
The strongest trap. It's flagged by 'therefore,' so it is a conclusion, but an intermediate one. It's used to show the coaches' ordering is wrong.
A premise. It supports the 'hour taken away' point, which in turn supports the main conclusion.
A concession. The author grants the coaches' fact before arguing against their advice.
Too strong. The author objects only to putting openings first, not to studying them ever.

questions.stimulus: Advocates of the proposed Varnet Act claim that extending copyright from 70 to 95 years after an author’s death will spur the creation of new works. But is there any reason to expect it to spur anything at all? An incentive can influence a decision only if the person deciding gives it some weight, and authors deciding whether to undertake a book give no weight to royalties that would begin accruing seven decades after their deaths. To be sure, the extension would enrich publishers who hold rights to older titles. Those titles, however, already exist, so whatever the extension does for them, it cannot have induced their creation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the extension would enrich publishers who hold rights to older titles?
choices: It is a premise offered in support of the argument’s conclusion that the extension would not spur the creation of new works.
It is presented as evidence that advocates of the extension are motivated by a desire to benefit publishers rather than authors.
It acknowledges a consequence of the extension that the argument goes on to maintain is not the benefit the extension’s advocates predict.
It is an intermediate conclusion that the argument supports by observing that the older titles already exist.
It is a claim that the argument attributes to the extension’s advocates and then rejects on the grounds that authors disregard distant royalties.
questions.explanation: Core move: locating a main conclusion stated as a rhetorical question (the extension gives no reason to expect new works) and then classifying a concession. ‘To be sure’ introduces an effect the author grants, and the next sentence neutralizes it: enriching holders of existing titles cannot have induced those titles’ creation, so it is not the predicted spur to new works (C). The most tempting trap is A, which correctly identifies the main conclusion but wrongly treats the concession as support; enriching publishers does nothing to show new works won’t be spurred, which is why the author must answer it. B imputes a motive the argument never discusses, D reverses the relationship (the ‘already exist’ point answers the claim rather than supporting it), and E is wrong because the advocates claim new works will be spurred, not that publishers will be enriched.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: There's no reason to expect the Varnet Act's extension to spur new works (stated as a rhetorical question).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: An incentive works only if the decider gives it weight; authors give no weight to royalties 70+ years after death; to be sure, publishers of older titles would gain, but those titles already exist, so the extension couldn't have caused their creation.

breakdown.analysis: The main conclusion hides in a rhetorical question: is there any reason to expect it to spur anything? Answer: no. 'To be sure' flags a concession: the extension does help someone, namely publishers of older titles. Then 'however' answers it: those books already exist, so helping them isn't the promised spur to new works. Concessions are things the author grants and then defuses, not reasons for the conclusion.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. It gets the main conclusion right but calls the concession support. Publishers getting richer does nothing to show new works won't appear. That's why the author has to answer it.
The argument never talks about the advocates' motives. This invents a point.

CORRECT. 'To be sure' grants that the extension would enrich publishers. The next sentence says that benefit goes to books that already exist, so it isn't the 'new works' benefit the advocates predict.
Reverses the relationship. The 'already exist' point answers this claim; it doesn't support it. And the claim isn't a conclusion at all.
The advocates claim new works will be spurred, not that publishers will be enriched. The author raises this point himself, and doesn't reject it; he grants it.

passages.title: Marrowfield's Four-Day School Week
passages.text:
Three years ago, the school district in the town of Marrowfield moved from a five-day to a four-day school week. Students now attend Monday through Thursday, and each school day has been lengthened by seventy minutes so that total instructional time is nearly unchanged. The district's main motive was financial: by closing its buildings on Fridays, it expected to save on heating, transportation, and substitute teachers.

By most measures, the change has worked. The district saved roughly six percent of its operating budget in the first year, and it used much of that money to raise teacher salaries, which had lagged behind those in neighboring districts. Teacher turnover, which had been the highest in the region, fell by nearly half. Test scores have stayed about where they were before the switch, neither rising nor falling noticeably.

The change has not been costless, however. Families in which every parent works on Fridays have had to find child care for that day, and for lower-income households this expense can consume a large share of the family budget. A town survey found that these families were far less satisfied with the new schedule than other families were. Marrowfield should therefore keep the four-day week but use part of its savings to fund supervised Friday programs at its schools, so that the benefits of the change are not purchased at the expense of the families least able to absorb its costs.
passages.subject: social-science

passages.title: The Sculptor Ilse Varnholt
passages.text:
For the first two decades of her career, the sculptor Ilse Varnholt worked almost exclusively in marble. Her pieces from this period—smooth, heavy torsos and slowly folding abstract forms—were carved over many months in a studio outside the port town of Kessling, and collectors prized them for their polish and their permanence. Varnholt herself described the work as an effort to “hold still” forms that seemed to her always on the verge of moving.

In 1994 a flood swept through her studio, destroying most of her tools and several unfinished pieces. When she resumed working two years later, she had abandoned stone entirely. Her new sculptures were built from unfired river clay and placed outdoors, along the very riverbank that had flooded, where rain and current gradually wore them away. Some lasted a season; a few dissolved within weeks. Varnholt photographed each piece at regular intervals until nothing of it remained.

Most critics treated this shift as a rupture, a renunciation of everything her marble work had stood for. Yet that reading overlooks how much the two bodies of work share. The marble pieces were never really about permanence: their surfaces were carved to suggest motion arrested mid-gesture, and Varnholt left visible chisel marks on many of them as a record of the hours of labor they contained. The clay works simply reverse the direction of the same inquiry. Rather than recording the time that went into making a form, they record the time it takes for a form to be unmade. What changed after the flood was not Varnholt's subject but the role she assigned to time—from something the sculptor spends on the work to something the world spends on it.

passages.title: Legal Rights in Digital Avatars
passages.text:
As online platforms allow users to build detailed digital avatars—animated figures that may reproduce a user's face, voice, and mannerisms—courts and legislatures have begun to confront a question that existing law did not anticipate: who holds rights in an avatar? Platforms have generally answered through their terms of service, which typically grant the platform a broad license to use, modify, and retain anything users create on it. Under this contractual approach, a user who leaves a platform may find that a replica of her own face continues to appear in its promotional materials.

Two alternatives have been proposed. The first treats an avatar as property belonging to the user who created it, much as a manuscript belongs to its author. Advocates of this view argue that it would let users transfer, sell, or delete their avatars as they choose. But the property model fits awkwardly with how avatars are actually made. Most avatars are assembled from templates, textures, and animation routines supplied by the platform, so the user's creative contribution is often slight; a property claim grounded in authorship would frequently give the user little or nothing.

The second alternative extends the right of publicity—the long-standing legal right of individuals to control commercial use of their name and likeness—to cover avatars that resemble their users. This approach does not depend on who authored an avatar's components; it protects the person the avatar depicts. Its proponents note that it would forbid precisely the practice that most troubles users: commercial exploitation of their likenesses after they have left a platform.

The publicity approach is the more promising of the two, but it has a limit its proponents rarely acknowledge. Many users deliberately build avatars that look nothing like themselves—a dragon, a cartoon fox, an idealized stranger. Such an avatar may carry a user's reputation as surely as a face does, especially in a community where the user has been known for years only by that figure; yet because it does not depict the user's likeness, the right of publicity as traditionally understood would not reach it. Any adequate legal regime will need some way of protecting identities that are built rather than inherited.

passages.title: The Color of Lake Teskel
passages.text:
For most of the twentieth century, Lake Teskel, a small alpine lake fed by the Orvald Glacier, was a pale, milky turquoise. Over the past fifteen years it has turned a deep blue-green. Two research groups have offered competing explanations for the change, and their dispute has become a minor proxy for a larger disagreement about how mountain lakes respond to a warming climate.

The hydrologist Mara Brandt and her colleagues attribute the change to the retreat of the Orvald Glacier. Glaciers grind bedrock into an extremely fine sediment, often called glacial flour, which meltwater carries into lakes; suspended in the water, these particles scatter light and produce the characteristic milky turquoise of glacier-fed lakes. As the Orvald has shrunk and its meltwater stream has shifted course, Brandt's group reports, the concentration of suspended sediment in Teskel has fallen by more than half. On their account, the lake is simply taking on the color that clear mountain water would have anyway.

The limnologist Tomas Ehrlund disputes this. Clear water, he notes, would be blue rather than blue-green; the green tint indicates phytoplankton, and his group's samples show chlorophyll concentrations roughly triple their levels of the 1990s. Ehrlund attributes the growth to warmer surface temperatures, which lengthen the season in which algae can multiply. Brandt's group, in reply, points out that the tripled concentrations are still low by the standards of lowland lakes and doubts that they could account for so marked a change in color.

Each side, it seems to me, has been too quick to treat the other's explanation as a rival rather than a partner. Glacial flour does more than tint the water: by scattering and absorbing light near the surface, it limits how deeply sunlight penetrates, and thus how much of the water column can support photosynthesis. A sharp decline in sediment would therefore by itself tend to promote algal growth, warming or no warming. If so, much of the chlorophyll increase Ehrlund documents may be a consequence of the very change Brandt identifies. This does not make warming irrelevant—Ehrlund's seasonal data suggest that it has lengthened the growing season—but it does mean that his chlorophyll measurements cannot, by themselves, establish warming as an independent cause of the change in color.

Admittedly, neither group has yet measured light penetration in the lake directly, and until someone does, this reconciliation remains a hypothesis rather than a finding. But it has the virtue of explaining both the loss of milkiness and the appearance of green, which neither account, taken alone, manages to do.

passages.title: Counterfactuals as Historical Evidence
passages.text:
Historians routinely make claims about what would have happened had things gone otherwise: that a treaty, if signed a year earlier, would have averted a war; that a dynasty would have remained secure had a harvest not failed. The philosopher Henrike Lasz has argued that such claims, however useful as rhetoric, can never function as evidence. Evidence, on her view, must be something that could in principle be observed, and a course of events that did not occur is by its nature unobservable. A counterfactual can thus be the conclusion of a historical argument—something one infers—but never a premise that lends support to some further claim.

Defenders of counterfactual history have generally replied by pointing to formal models. The economic historian Dov Arranz, for instance, has estimated what a region's grain output would have been without a particular canal by modeling transport costs, and he treats the resulting figure as evidence of the canal's importance. Lasz's response is that Arranz's figure is only as good as the assumptions built into his model, and that those assumptions have never been tested against any observation of a world without the canal.

Lasz is right about this, but less follows from it than she supposes. Every inference from evidence relies on assumptions not tested against the very case at hand: a historian who dates a manuscript by its ink relies on assumptions about how inks age that were established on other documents. That Arranz's assumptions are untested against the counterfactual world is therefore not what distinguishes his figure from ordinary evidence. What does distinguish it is subtler. The ink-dating historian's assumptions were tested on cases in which the outcome they predict was eventually observed; Arranz's model, by contrast, can be calibrated only against the world in which the canal was built.

This suggests that the dispute has been mislocated. The question is not whether counterfactuals may serve as premises—once adequately supported, any claim may—but whether the support for a given counterfactual ever reaches beyond the single history we have. Where a counterfactual rests on regularities observed across many comparable cases—how harvest failures have affected many dynasties, say—it can carry genuine evidential weight, not because it describes something observed but because the regularity it applies was observed. Where it rests only on a model fitted to the one case under study, it adds nothing that the model's inputs did not already contain, and treating it as independent evidence counts the same information twice.

None of this vindicates counterfactual history wholesale, and Arranz's canal estimate, as it happens, falls on the wrong side of the line. But Lasz's criterion, which would disqualify every counterfactual alike, cannot distinguish the cases in which historians are genuinely learning something from those in which they are merely restating their assumptions.
