questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Marrowfield's four-day school week has saved the district money, but it has harmed student achievement.
Marrowfield's switch to a four-day school week was motivated mainly by a desire to raise teacher salaries.
Marrowfield's four-day week has largely succeeded, but the town should use some of its savings to ease its burden on certain families.
Four-day school weeks reduce teacher turnover and should be adopted by districts that have difficulty retaining teachers.
Marrowfield should return to a five-day school week because lower-income families cannot afford child care on Fridays.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim the whole passage builds toward, here the recommendation in the last sentence together with the overall verdict that the change has worked. C captures both halves: the change has worked, and the town should fund Friday programs for the families it burdens. The most tempting trap is E, because the third paragraph dwells on the child-care burden; but the author explicitly says Marrowfield should keep the four-day week, so E reverses the recommendation. A contradicts the passage's statement that test scores have held steady.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the sentence that sums up the whole passage: what the author is ultimately arguing.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2's verdict ('by most measures, the change has worked') and the recommendation in the last sentence of paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: The passage goes: here's the change, it worked, but it hurts some families, so keep it and fix that. The main point has to carry both halves: success plus a targeted fix. Answers that grab only one paragraph, or flip the recommendation, are out.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. Test scores stayed about the same, so there's no harm to achievement.
Wrong motive. The district's main motive was saving money. Raising salaries is what it did with the savings.
CORRECT. It gets both halves: the change has largely worked, and the town should use some savings to help the families it burdens. That's where the whole passage is headed.
Too broad. The author talks only about Marrowfield and never recommends four-day weeks for other districts.
The most tempting trap, because paragraph 3 dwells on child-care costs. But the author says to keep the four-day week. E reverses the recommendation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following occurred after Marrowfield adopted the four-day school week?
choices: Teacher turnover in the district declined substantially.
Test scores in the district rose noticeably.
The district reduced its total instructional time by about one-fifth.
The district closed its schools on Mondays to save on heating costs.
Teacher salaries in the district fell below those in neighboring districts.
questions.explanation: Core move: locate a stated fact. The second paragraph says turnover 'fell by nearly half,' which A restates. The most tempting trap is C, because dropping one day of five sounds like losing one-fifth of class time; but the passage says each day was lengthened by seventy minutes so that total instructional time is 'nearly unchanged.' E reverses the salary facts, since salaries were raised from below those of neighboring districts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find something the passage says happened after the switch.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (results), plus paragraph 1 for the instructional-time detail.

breakdown.analysis: Detail questions are lookup jobs. Paragraph 2 lists the results: six percent savings, raised salaries, turnover nearly halved, scores flat. Match one of those, and watch for answers that sound logical but contradict a specific line.

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 2 says turnover 'fell by nearly half.' That's a substantial decline.
Contradicts the passage. Scores stayed about the same, 'neither rising nor falling noticeably.'

The most tempting trap. Dropping one of five days sounds like losing a fifth of class time. But each day got seventy minutes longer, so total time is 'nearly unchanged.' Don't do math the passage already did for you.
Wrong day. Schools close on Fridays.
Reversed. Salaries had lagged behind neighbors, and the district raised them.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The savings produced by the four-day week were too small to justify the inconvenience it has caused families.
The lengthened school day is the main reason test scores in Marrowfield have remained stable.
Families in which a parent is at home on Fridays are generally dissatisfied with the new schedule.
The district should stop using its savings to raise teacher salaries.
A policy that benefits a community overall can place a disproportionate burden on some members, which the community should try to lessen.
questions.explanation: Core move: infer the general principle behind the author's recommendation. The author praises the change overall yet asks the town to protect 'the families least able to absorb its costs,' which is exactly the principle in E. The most tempting trap is B: the passage mentions both the longer day and the stable scores, but it never says one caused the other. C misreads the survey, which found working families less satisfied than other families, and D goes beyond the author's request to use only 'part' of the savings.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author would likely agree with, based on what the author says.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, especially the final recommendation about 'the families least able to absorb its costs.'

breakdown.analysis: The author likes the policy overall but wants the people it hurts protected. Pull out the general principle behind that: a good policy can hit some people harder, and the community should ease that. Inference answers must be backed by the text, not just plausible.

choices.note: Opposite of the author. The author says the change worked and wants to keep it, so the savings did justify it.
The most tempting trap. The passage mentions both the longer day and the stable scores, but never says one caused the other. You can't pick an answer on a possibility.
Misreads the survey. It found working families less satisfied than others. It says nothing about at-home families being dissatisfied.
Goes too far. The author wants only 'part' of the savings for Friday programs, and never objects to the raises.

CORRECT. The author praises the change overall but wants to protect 'the families least able to absorb its costs.' That's this principle: an overall good policy can burden some people more, and the town should lessen that.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Marrowfield's four-day school week is best described as
choices: unqualified enthusiasm for the change
approval tempered by concern about its effects on certain families
reluctant acceptance of a policy the author considers mostly harmful
neutral detachment, offering no evaluation of the policy
strong disapproval, softened only by recognition of its financial savings
questions.explanation: Core move: match both the direction and the strength of the author's view. The author says 'by most measures, the change has worked' and wants to keep it, but also says it 'has not been costless' for some families; B captures that qualified approval. The most tempting trap is A, since the author clearly favors the policy; but the third paragraph's concern and proposed remedy rule out 'unqualified.' C and E get the direction wrong, and D ignores the explicit recommendation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about the four-day week: which direction, and how strongly.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 ('by most measures, the change has worked') and paragraph 3 ('has not been costless' and the recommendation).

breakdown.analysis: Get the direction first: positive. The author wants to keep it. Then the strength: not total, because the author worries about some families and proposes a fix. So: approval with a reservation.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. The author does favor the policy, but paragraph 3's concern and proposed fix rule out 'unqualified.'
CORRECT. The author says it has worked and should be kept (approval) but flags the child-care burden on some families (the concern).
Wrong direction. The author thinks the policy mostly worked, not that it's mostly harmful.
The author makes a clear recommendation. That's not neutral.
Wrong direction. The author approves of the policy and wants to keep it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: Two phases of an artist's career are described, and the author argues that the later phase is artistically superior to the earlier one.
A change in an artist's practice is described, its cause is debated, and the author concludes that the cause cannot be determined.
An artist's early work is described, critics' praise of that work is summarized, and the author explains why that praise was misplaced.
A change in an artist's practice is described, and the author endorses the prevailing critical account of that change while adding further evidence for it.
An artist's earlier and later practices are described, and the author then challenges a common interpretation of the change by identifying a continuity between them.
questions.explanation: Core move: track what each paragraph does, especially the turn signaled by 'Yet.' Paragraphs one and two describe the marble and clay periods; paragraph three rejects the critics' 'rupture' reading by showing that both bodies of work concern time, which is E. The most tempting trap is D, which correctly notes a prevailing critical account but reverses the author's relation to it: the author challenges it rather than endorsing it. A is wrong because the author never ranks the two phases.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what each part of the passage does, in order.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All three paragraphs; the turn is 'Yet' in paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 1: the marble years. Paragraph 2: the flood and the switch to clay. Paragraph 3: critics call it a break, 'Yet' the author says that misses a shared thread: both bodies of work are about time. So: two phases, then the author challenges the common reading by pointing to continuity.

choices.note: The author never says one phase is better. The point is that they're connected, not ranked.
The cause (the flood) isn't debated, and the author does reach a conclusion. Wrong on both counts.
The critics in the passage talk about the change, not praise for the early work. And the author doesn't call collectors' taste 'misplaced' as the main move.
The most tempting trap. There is a prevailing critical account, but the author challenges it with 'Yet.' D flips the author's stance.

CORRECT. The earlier and later work are described in paragraphs 1 and 2. Paragraph 3 rejects the 'rupture' reading by showing both concern time. That's challenging a common view by finding a continuity.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Varnholt's clay sculptures
choices: were fired in a kiln so that they could withstand outdoor conditions for at least a season
were produced in the same studio near Kessling in which she had carved her marble pieces
were carved to suggest motion arrested mid-gesture, as her marble pieces had been
were photographed at intervals over the course of their deterioration
were placed along the riverbank in order to protect them from future flooding
questions.explanation: Core move: find the detail and reject phrases borrowed from elsewhere in the passage. The second paragraph says Varnholt photographed each clay piece 'at regular intervals until nothing of it remained,' which D paraphrases. The most tempting trap is C, which quotes the passage's own words, but 'motion arrested mid-gesture' describes the marble pieces, not the clay ones. A contradicts 'unfired,' and E reverses the point: the pieces were placed there so that the water would wear them away.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about the clay sculptures.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2: unfired river clay, placed along the flooded bank, worn away by rain and current, photographed at intervals until nothing remained. Be careful with answers that borrow words from the marble paragraphs and pin them on the clay.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. The clay was 'unfired,' and some pieces lasted only weeks.
Not stated. The flood destroyed the studio's tools, and the clay pieces were placed outdoors by the river. Nothing says she used the Kessling studio.
The most tempting trap. It uses the passage's own words, but 'motion arrested mid-gesture' describes the marble pieces, not the clay ones.
CORRECT. She 'photographed each piece at regular intervals until nothing of it remained.' D says the same thing.
Reversed. She put them by the river so the water would wear them away, not to protect them.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements about Varnholt's marble works?
choices: They were valued by collectors chiefly because they showed visible traces of the labor that produced them.
Their appeal to collectors rested partly on a quality that, in the author's view, was not central to what the works were about.
They addressed the theme of time less successfully than her later clay works did.
They were completed more quickly than her later clay works were.
Most of them were destroyed in the 1994 flood that struck her studio.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine two paragraphs. The first says collectors prized the marble pieces for their 'polish and their permanence'; the third says those pieces 'were never really about permanence.' Together these yield B. The most tempting trap is A, which uses the passage's chisel-mark detail but attaches it to the wrong party: the author, not the collectors, sees the marks as a record of labor. C invents a comparison the author never makes, and E overstates the flood damage, which the passage limits to 'several unfinished pieces.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement about the marble works the author would likely agree with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (collectors prized 'polish and permanence') and paragraph 3 (the marble 'was never really about permanence').

breakdown.analysis: Put two lines together. Collectors liked the marble partly for its permanence. The author says the marble wasn't really about permanence. So collectors valued something the author thinks wasn't the point. It's like loving a protest song for its catchy tune.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. Chisel marks are in the passage, but the author is the one who reads them as a record of labor. Collectors prized polish and permanence. Wrong party.

CORRECT. Collectors prized permanence (paragraph 1), and the author says the marble 'was never really about permanence' (paragraph 3). So part of the appeal rested on something the author sees as beside the point.
No comparison of success. The author says the clay reverses the same inquiry, not that it handles time better.
Unsupported. The marble pieces took many months, but the passage never says how long the clay pieces took to make. No basis for the comparison.
Overstates the flood. It destroyed tools and 'several unfinished pieces,' not most of her marble work.

questions.stem: The author mentions the visible chisel marks on many of Varnholt's marble pieces primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the polish that collectors prized in her early work
suggest that many of her marble pieces were left unfinished
support the claim that her marble work was concerned with time rather than with permanence
explain why critics regarded her turn to clay as a rupture
show that Varnholt valued technical skill above expressive content
questions.explanation: Core move: identify the role a detail plays in the author's argument. The chisel marks appear right after the claim that the marble pieces 'were never really about permanence,' as evidence that they record 'the hours of labor they contained,' that is, time spent. So C is right. The most tempting trap is B, which borrows 'unfinished' from the flood paragraph, but visible tool marks were a deliberate choice, not a sign of incompleteness. A is the opposite of the point, since chisel marks work against polish.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the chisel marks: what job they do in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the sentence right after 'The marble pieces were never really about permanence.'

breakdown.analysis: Function questions ask 'why is this here?' The chisel marks come right after the claim that the marble wasn't about permanence. They're a 'record of the hours of labor': time spent. So they're evidence that the marble work was about time. Look at the claim the detail sits next to.

choices.note: Opposite of the point. Chisel marks are rough, not polished. They work against the idea of a smooth surface.
The most tempting trap. It borrows 'unfinished' from the flood paragraph. But the marks were left on purpose as a record of labor, not a sign the pieces weren't done.
CORRECT. The marks record 'the hours of labor' in each piece, so they back up the claim that the marble work was about time, not permanence.
The marks are the author's evidence against the critics' rupture reading, not an explanation of it.
The author never ranks skill against expression. The marks are about time, not technique.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The publicity approach is preferable to the property model, but as traditionally understood it would not protect identities carried by avatars that do not resemble their users.
The right of publicity should replace platforms' terms of service as the basis for determining rights in avatars, because it protects users regardless of who authored an avatar's components.
Treating avatars as users' property would give users the greatest control over their avatars, but it would conflict with the licenses granted to platforms by their terms of service.
Because most avatars are assembled from templates and routines supplied by platforms, the platforms rather than the users should hold the rights in them.
Existing law is incapable of resolving disputes over avatars, so legislatures must create an entirely new category of rights to govern them.
questions.explanation: Core move: state the author's conclusion with its qualification intact. The final paragraph ranks the publicity approach above the property model and then names its limit, so A captures both parts. The most tempting trap is B, which gets the preference right but drops the limit, and the final paragraph exists precisely to state that limit. E inflates the last sentence: the author calls for 'some way' of protecting built identities, not a wholly new body of law, and never says existing law can resolve nothing.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the sentence that sums up the author's overall argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the ranking ('more promising') and the limit that follows.

breakdown.analysis: The passage lays out a problem, two fixes, and then a verdict: publicity beats property, but publicity misses avatars that don't look like their users. The main point needs both the preference and the limit. An answer that keeps only half is a trap.

choices.note: CORRECT. It has both parts of the final paragraph: publicity is better than property, but as traditionally understood it won't protect avatars that don't resemble their users.
The most tempting trap. Right preference, but it drops the limit, which is the whole reason the last paragraph exists.
The author says the property model would often give users little or nothing, not the greatest control. And the conflict with terms of service isn't the point.
The author never says platforms should hold the rights. The templates point is only used to show the property model's weakness.
Inflates the last sentence. The author asks for 'some way' to protect built identities, not a whole new category of rights, and never says existing law can't help at all.

questions.stem: According to the passage, advocates of the property model claim that it would
choices: protect users whose avatars bear no resemblance to them
prevent platforms from supplying templates and animation routines to users
allow users to dispose of their avatars as they see fit
protect the person an avatar depicts regardless of who authored the avatar's components
reflect the way in which most avatars are actually made
questions.explanation: Core move: match a paraphrase to the correct party's claim. Advocates say the model would let users 'transfer, sell, or delete their avatars as they choose,' which C restates as disposing of them as users see fit. The most tempting trap is D, which nearly quotes the passage, but that is the description of the publicity approach in the third paragraph. E reverses the author's objection that the property model 'fits awkwardly with how avatars are actually made,' and A is the author's own concern about the publicity approach.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what supporters of the property model say it would do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the sentence beginning 'Advocates of this view argue.'

breakdown.analysis: The passage says advocates believe the property model would let users 'transfer, sell, or delete their avatars as they choose.' Find the paraphrase. Watch for claims that belong to a different party or a different approach.

choices.note: Wrong party and wrong approach. That's the author's concern about the publicity approach, in paragraph 4.
Nobody claims this. Templates are mentioned only as a reason the property model fits awkwardly.
CORRECT. 'Transfer, sell, or delete their avatars as they choose' is exactly disposing of them as users see fit.
The most tempting trap. It nearly quotes the passage, but that's how paragraph 3 describes the publicity approach, not the property model.
Reversed. The author says the property model 'fits awkwardly with how avatars are actually made.'

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that a user who has assembled a cartoon-fox avatar entirely from a platform's stock templates, and who has been known in an online community only by that avatar for years,
choices: would be adequately protected under the right of publicity, since the avatar carries the user's reputation
would have a strong claim under the property model, since the avatar has come to represent the user
has no interest in the avatar that the law ought to recognize
would gain little protection from either proposed alternative, despite having an interest that the author believes the law should protect
would be better protected under the platform's terms of service than under the right of publicity
questions.explanation: Core move: apply two paragraphs to one new case. The second paragraph implies that a user whose creative contribution is slight gets 'little or nothing' under the authorship-based property model, and the fourth says the traditional right of publicity would not reach a non-resembling avatar, though the author thinks such identities need protection; D combines both. The most tempting trap is A, because the author says such an avatar 'may carry a user's reputation as surely as a face does'; but the author says that to show a gap in the publicity right, not to show that it covers this user. C reverses the author's view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's views to a new case: a cartoon-fox avatar built only from stock templates, known in a community for years.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (property model gives little to users who contributed little) and paragraph 4 (publicity doesn't reach non-resembling avatars, but such identities need protection).

breakdown.analysis: Run the case through both approaches. Property model: grounded in authorship, and this user authored almost nothing, so little or nothing. Publicity: protects likeness, and a cartoon fox doesn't look like the user, so it doesn't reach. But the author says built identities like this one deserve protection. So: a real interest, and neither approach covers it.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. The author does say such an avatar can carry a reputation, but says it to point out a gap: the publicity right as traditionally understood won't reach it. A turns the gap into coverage.
Wrong. The property model rests on authorship, and this user built it entirely from stock templates. The author says that gives 'little or nothing.'
Reverses the author's view. The final sentence says the law needs a way to protect identities that are built rather than inherited.

CORRECT. Stock templates mean little under the property model; no resemblance means the traditional publicity right doesn't reach it. Yet the author thinks this kind of built identity should be protected.
The author presents terms of service as the problem, since they let platforms keep using what users create. Nothing suggests they'd protect this user better.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward the publicity approach?
choices: wholehearted endorsement of it as a complete solution to the problem of avatar rights
skepticism that it would actually prevent platforms from using users' likenesses after they leave
preference for it over the contractual approach, but not over the property model
rejection of it on the grounds that it ignores who authored an avatar's components
qualified approval, combined with the view that it is incomplete
questions.explanation: Core move: measure the author's exact degree of commitment. The author calls the publicity approach 'the more promising of the two' but says it 'has a limit,' which is qualified approval of an incomplete approach, as in E. The most tempting trap is A, since the author does prefer the approach, but 'complete solution' contradicts the limit the final paragraph identifies. D turns a strength into an objection: the approach's independence from authorship is something the author presents neutrally, as a feature, and C reverses the ranking.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about the publicity approach: direction and strength.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: 'the more promising of the two, but it has a limit.'

breakdown.analysis: Direction: positive. It's 'the more promising' option. Strength: limited. It has a gap the author spends a whole paragraph on. So: approval with a reservation, and the reservation is that it's incomplete.

choices.note: The most tempting trap. The author does prefer it, but 'complete solution' clashes with the limit the final paragraph spells out.
The author never doubts it would stop platforms using likenesses. The proponents say it forbids exactly that, and the author doesn't push back on it.
Reverses the ranking. The author prefers publicity over the property model; 'the two' are the two alternatives.
Turns a strength into an objection. Not depending on authorship is presented as a feature, and the author doesn't reject the approach.
CORRECT. 'More promising' is the approval; 'has a limit' and the need for some way to protect built identities show the author thinks it's incomplete.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The change in Lake Teskel's color is due primarily to the retreat of the Orvald Glacier and the resulting loss of suspended sediment, rather than to rising surface temperatures.
Ehrlund's chlorophyll measurements show that warming has been an independent cause of the change in Lake Teskel's color.
Neither the decline in glacial sediment nor the growth of phytoplankton can explain the change in Lake Teskel's color.
The two explanations for the lake's change in color are better seen as connected than as competing, since the decline in sediment may itself have promoted the algal growth Ehrlund emphasizes.
Until light penetration in Lake Teskel is measured directly, no explanation of the change in its color should be preferred to any other.
questions.explanation: Core move: recognize that the author's thesis reframes the debate rather than picking a winner, and keep its hedges. The fourth paragraph opens by calling the explanations partners rather than rivals and argues that the sediment decline may drive algal growth, which is D. The strongest trap is A: the reconciliation does make the glacier's retreat look more basic, but the author never says 'primarily,' grants that warming has lengthened the growing season, and rejects the 'rather than' framing. E inflates the concession: the author grants that the proposal is unconfirmed but still argues that it has an explanatory advantage, so the author does not hold all explanations equal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the sentence that sums up the author's overall argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4's opening sentence and its reasoning, plus the hedge in paragraph 5.

breakdown.analysis: Two groups fight: Brandt says less sediment, Ehrlund says more algae from warming. The author says they're partners, not rivals: less sediment lets more light in, which grows more algae. So the author reframes the debate rather than picking a winner, and keeps it hedged ('may'). The right answer needs the 'connected, not competing' idea.

choices.note: The strongest trap. The author's link does make the glacier look more basic, but never says 'primarily,' grants that warming lengthened the growing season, and rejects the 'rather than' framing.
Opposite of the author. The author says the chlorophyll data 'cannot, by themselves' show warming is an independent cause.
Too negative. The author says each explanation is part of the story and together they explain both changes.
CORRECT. Paragraph 4 opens by calling the explanations partners, not rivals, and argues the sediment drop may itself have boosted the algae. That's the author's thesis, with the right hedge.
Inflates the concession. The author admits the idea is unconfirmed but still argues it explains more than either account alone. So the author doesn't treat all explanations as equal.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a claim made by Brandt's group?
choices: Warmer surface temperatures have lengthened the season in which algae can multiply in Lake Teskel.
Phytoplankton concentrations that remain low by the standards of lowland lakes are unlikely to account for so pronounced a change in Lake Teskel's color.
A decline in suspended sediment would by itself tend to promote algal growth in Lake Teskel.
Clear mountain water would be blue rather than blue-green.
The Orvald Glacier's meltwater stream has carried more glacial flour into Lake Teskel as the glacier has retreated.
questions.explanation: Core move: attribute each claim to the right party when three voices share the same vocabulary. B paraphrases Brandt's reply that the tripled concentrations 'are still low by the standards of lowland lakes' and that they doubt such levels 'could account for so marked a change.' The most tempting trap is D: Brandt's group does speak of the color 'clear mountain water would have,' but the specific claim that clear water would be blue rather than blue-green is Ehrlund's objection to Brandt. C is the author's own claim and A is Ehrlund's, while E reverses Brandt's report that sediment has fallen.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim made specifically by Brandt's group.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Brandt's account) and the last sentence of paragraph 3 (Brandt's reply to Ehrlund).

breakdown.analysis: Three voices talk about the same things: Brandt, Ehrlund, and the author. Tag each claim with who said it. Brandt: sediment fell, the lake is just showing clear water's color, and tripled chlorophyll is still too low to matter much. Ehrlund: clear water would be blue, not blue-green; warming lengthens the algae season. Author: less sediment would itself boost algae.

choices.note: That's Ehrlund's claim, about warmer surface temperatures.
CORRECT. Brandt's group replies that the tripled levels are 'still low by the standards of lowland lakes' and doubts they 'could account for so marked a change.' B paraphrases that.
That's the author's own claim in paragraph 4, not Brandt's.
The most tempting trap. Brandt's group mentions the color clear water would have, but saying clear water would be blue, not blue-green, is Ehrlund's objection to Brandt.
Reversed. Brandt reports that suspended sediment fell by more than half.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Ehrlund's chlorophyll data are less damaging to Brandt's explanation than Ehrlund takes them to be.
Brandt's group is correct that the tripled chlorophyll concentrations are too low to affect the color of Lake Teskel.
Warming has had no measurable effect on the length of the algal growing season in Lake Teskel.
The loss of Lake Teskel's milkiness is better explained by Ehrlund's account than by Brandt's.
If light penetration in Lake Teskel were measured and found to be unchanged, Brandt's account of the lake's color change would be refuted.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine Ehrlund's use of the data in the third paragraph with the author's reinterpretation of it in the fourth. Ehrlund offers the chlorophyll rise as evidence against Brandt, but the author argues that 'much of the chlorophyll increase' may be caused by Brandt's own mechanism, so the data fit her account better than Ehrlund assumes; that is A, stated indirectly. The most tempting trap is B, since the author does treat Ehrlund's data cautiously; but the author's reconciliation credits the algae with 'the appearance of green,' so the author thinks they do affect the color. E is a near miss: unchanged light penetration would undercut the author's proposed link, not Brandt's sediment account of the lost milkiness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author would likely agree with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (Ehrlund uses chlorophyll against Brandt) and paragraph 4 (the author reinterprets that data).

breakdown.analysis: Ehrlund thinks his chlorophyll numbers hurt Brandt's sediment story. The author says much of that chlorophyll increase may come from Brandt's own mechanism: less sediment, more light, more algae. So the data don't hurt Brandt as much as Ehrlund thinks. It's like a rival lawyer's star witness who turns out to help your case.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author argues much of the chlorophyll rise may be caused by the sediment drop Brandt identifies. So Ehrlund's data actually fit Brandt's account and do less damage than Ehrlund supposes.
The most tempting trap. The author is cautious about Ehrlund's conclusions, but credits the algae with 'the appearance of green.' So the author thinks they do affect the color.
Contradicts the author, who says Ehrlund's seasonal data suggest warming has lengthened the growing season.
Wrong. The loss of milkiness is Brandt's part of the story (less sediment), not Ehrlund's.
Near miss. Unchanged light penetration would undercut the author's link between sediment and algae. It wouldn't refute Brandt's account that less sediment removed the milkiness.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the function of the first sentence of the last paragraph (the sentence beginning 'Admittedly')?
choices: It casts doubt on the sediment measurements reported by Brandt's group.
It indicates that the author's proposed reconciliation should be abandoned unless further evidence is found.
It suggests that both research groups have neglected a measurement that would decide which of their accounts is correct.
It acknowledges that a link on which the author's proposal depends has not yet been empirically confirmed.
It identifies a reason for preferring Ehrlund's account to Brandt's.
questions.explanation: Core move: identify a concession and its exact target. The author's reconciliation depends on sediment limiting light penetration, and the sentence admits that light penetration has not been measured, so the proposal 'remains a hypothesis'; D describes this. The strongest trap is C: the sentence does say neither group has made the measurement, but that measurement would test the author's link between the accounts, and the author denies that they are rivals to be decided between. B overstates the concession, which the next sentence immediately follows by defending the hypothesis.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the 'Admittedly' sentence does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5 and the light-penetration link in paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: The author's idea depends on one link: sediment limits how deep light reaches. 'Admittedly' concedes that nobody has measured light penetration, so the idea is still a hypothesis. Then 'But' defends it anyway. So the sentence is a concession about an unconfirmed link in the author's own proposal.

choices.note: Brandt's sediment numbers aren't questioned. The missing data is about light penetration.
Too strong. The very next sentence defends the hypothesis. The author doesn't say drop it.
The strongest trap. The sentence does say neither group made the measurement, but the measurement would test the author's link, not settle which group wins. The author denies they're rivals.
CORRECT. The proposal depends on sediment limiting light, and the author admits light penetration hasn't been measured, so the idea 'remains a hypothesis.'
Nothing here favors Ehrlund. It's about the author's own proposal.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Lasz is mistaken in holding that counterfactual claims are unobservable, since counterfactuals grounded in regularities across many cases describe events that were in fact observed.
A counterfactual's evidential value depends not on its unobservability but on whether its support reaches beyond the single case studied, a distinction Lasz's criterion misses.
Lasz is right that counterfactual claims can never serve as premises, but she is wrong to deny that Arranz's canal estimate has evidential value.
Because every inference relies on assumptions untested against the case at hand, counterfactual claims are as legitimate as evidence as any other historical claims.
Formal models such as Arranz's provide the most reliable means by which historians can support counterfactual claims.
questions.explanation: Core move: separate the author's thesis from the intermediate steps and from the views attributed to others. The author argues that the real question is whether a counterfactual's support 'reaches beyond the single history we have' and ends by faulting Lasz's criterion for being unable to make that distinction, which is B. The strongest trap is D: the third paragraph's point about untested assumptions is the author's, but it is only an intermediate step, and the final paragraph says 'none of this vindicates counterfactual history wholesale.' A uses the passage's own words in the wrong relationship, since the author says such a counterfactual carries weight 'not because it describes something observed' but because the regularity it applies was observed. C reverses both of the author's positions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the sentence that sums up the author's overall argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4 ('the dispute has been mislocated') and paragraph 5 (the final verdict on Lasz).

breakdown.analysis: Lasz: counterfactuals can't be evidence because you can't observe them. The author: that's the wrong test. What matters is whether a counterfactual's support reaches beyond the one case, such as regularities seen across many cases. Lasz's rule can't tell the good cases from the bad. Note the intermediate steps (everyone uses untested assumptions) aren't the main point.

choices.note: Uses the passage's words the wrong way. The author says such counterfactuals carry weight 'not because it describes something observed' but because the regularity was observed. The author doesn't deny they're unobservable.
CORRECT. The author moves the question from observability to whether support reaches beyond the single history, then faults Lasz's criterion for missing that difference.
Reverses both positions. The author says counterfactuals can be premises, and agrees Arranz's estimate fails.
The strongest trap. The untested-assumptions point is the author's, but it's a stepping stone, and the end says 'none of this vindicates counterfactual history wholesale.'
Opposite. Arranz's model is the example that falls on the wrong side of the line.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the assumptions underlying the ink-dating historian's inference differ from those underlying Arranz's model in that the former
choices: were tested against the particular manuscript that the historian is attempting to date
have not been tested against the very case to which they are applied
derive from a model calibrated against the world as it actually developed
rest on regularities observed in the histories of many dynasties
were confirmed in instances where the result they would predict could later be checked
questions.explanation: Core move: answer the exact question asked, which is a difference and not a similarity, and match a paraphrase. The passage says the ink-dater's assumptions 'were tested on cases in which the outcome they predict was eventually observed,' while Arranz's model can be calibrated only against the actual world; E paraphrases the first half of that contrast. The strongest trap is B, which is true of the ink-dater's assumptions but is a feature the author says they share with Arranz's ('every inference' relies on such assumptions), so it cannot be the difference. A contradicts the passage, C describes Arranz's model, and D moves the harvest example from the fourth paragraph into the wrong comparison.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how the ink-dater's assumptions differ from Arranz's.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of paragraph 3: 'What does distinguish it is subtler.'

breakdown.analysis: The question asks for a difference, not a similarity. Both rely on assumptions not tested on the case at hand; that's shared. The difference: ink-dating assumptions were tested on cases where the predicted outcome was later observed, while Arranz's model can only be calibrated on the real world, where the canal was built.

choices.note: Contradicts the passage. The ink assumptions were established on other documents, not this one.
The strongest trap. True of the ink-dater, but the author says it's true of every inference, Arranz's included. A shared feature can't be the difference.
That describes Arranz's model, not the ink-dater's assumptions.
Wrong example. The many-dynasties point is from paragraph 4 and isn't about ink dating.
CORRECT. The ink assumptions 'were tested on cases in which the outcome they predict was eventually observed.' Arranz's can't be. That's the difference.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that both the author and Lasz would accept which one of the following?
choices: A counterfactual claim can serve as a premise in a historical argument provided that it has been adequately supported.
Counterfactuals grounded in regularities observed across many comparable cases can carry genuine evidential weight.
Arranz's estimate of the region's grain output without the canal should not be treated as independent evidence of the canal's importance.
Every inference from evidence relies on assumptions that have not been tested against the case at hand.
The untested assumptions built into Arranz's model are what distinguish his figure from ordinary evidence.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the claim two parties share for different reasons, using the first and second paragraphs for Lasz and the fourth and fifth for the author. Lasz holds that no counterfactual can be evidence, so she would reject Arranz's figure as evidence of any kind; the author says the estimate 'falls on the wrong side of the line,' where treating a counterfactual 'as independent evidence counts the same information twice.' Only C follows from both views. The strongest trap is A, which is the author's explicit view ('once adequately supported, any claim may'), but it is exactly what Lasz denies. E is Lasz's implicit position, which the author expressly rejects, and B and D are the author's views alone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim both the author and Lasz would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 1 and 2 for Lasz; paragraphs 4 and 5 for the author.

breakdown.analysis: Common ground can come from different reasons. Lasz: no counterfactual is ever evidence, so Arranz's figure isn't either. Author: Arranz's figure rests on a model fitted to one case, so treating it as independent evidence counts the same information twice. Different routes, same verdict on Arranz. Every other answer is one side's view only.

choices.note: The strongest trap. That's the author's view ('once adequately supported, any claim may'), but Lasz says a counterfactual can never be a premise.
Author only. Lasz rejects counterfactuals as evidence, period.

CORRECT. Lasz rejects all counterfactual evidence, so she rejects this one. The author says Arranz's estimate 'falls on the wrong side of the line' and counts the same information twice. Both reject it as independent evidence.
Author only. It's the author's point in paragraph 3, and nothing shows Lasz accepts it.
That's the position the author explicitly rejects: untested assumptions are 'not what distinguishes his figure from ordinary evidence.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Lasz's position is best described as
choices: endorsement of her verdict on one particular case, together with a denial that her standard tracks the distinction that actually matters
acceptance of her criterion for what counts as evidence, together with doubt that it applies to estimates derived from formal models
rejection of her claim that Arranz's assumptions are untested, together with agreement that counterfactuals cannot be premises
broad agreement with her conclusions, qualified by concern that she has overstated the importance of observability in a few cases
agreement that counterfactuals can never be evidence, together with the view that they are nonetheless indispensable to historical argument
questions.explanation: Core move: measure a split attitude, agreeing on an outcome while rejecting the reasoning behind it. The author grants that 'Lasz is right about this' and that Arranz's estimate fails, but says her criterion 'cannot distinguish' the cases that matter, which is the indirectly worded A. The strongest trap is D, which sounds suitably moderate, but the author does not broadly agree with Lasz's conclusions: the author rejects her central claim that counterfactuals can never be premises, not just an emphasis 'in a few cases.' E invents a middle position that contradicts the author's claim that some counterfactuals 'carry genuine evidential weight,' and C has the author rejecting a point the author explicitly concedes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about Lasz's position.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 ('Lasz is right about this, but less follows') and paragraph 5 (her criterion 'cannot distinguish' the cases).

breakdown.analysis: Split attitude. The author agrees with Lasz's verdict on Arranz (it fails) but rejects her rule: banning all counterfactuals misses the real dividing line. So: agree on the outcome in one case, disagree about the standard. It's like agreeing a referee made the right call on one play while saying his rulebook is wrong.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author agrees Arranz's estimate fails (her verdict on one case) but says her criterion 'cannot distinguish' the cases where historians really learn something (it misses the distinction that matters).
The author doesn't accept her criterion. The whole point is that unobservability is the wrong test.
Backwards on both. The author concedes 'Lasz is right about this' on the untested assumptions, and says counterfactuals can be premises.
The strongest trap, because it sounds moderate. But the author rejects her central claim that counterfactuals can never be premises. That's not 'broad agreement.'
Contradicts the author, who says some counterfactuals 'carry genuine evidential weight.'
